caption: The galaxy NGC 1275 and its gas filaments, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Reddish, lace-like threads wrap around the bright galaxy at the centre of this picture. The galaxy is NGC 1275, the giant elliptical at the heart of a galaxy cluster in the constellation Perseus, and the threads are fragile filaments of gas that Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys captured in fine detail.

The filaments stay cool even though the gas around them sits at roughly 55 million degrees Celsius. A magnetic field holds them together. By studying their shape, astronomers were able to estimate that field's strength for the first time, and showed how magnetism has kept the filaments from collapsing under gravity or being torn apart by the turbulent cluster over their lifetime of about 100 million years.

The filaments also reveal how energy from the galaxy's central black hole is passed on to the surrounding gas. Hubble could even separate individual threads only about 200 light-years wide, while whole filaments can stretch to 200 000 light-years.
explore: The entire frame spans roughly 260 000 light-years. The dark dust lanes belong to a separate spiral galaxy lying partly in front of NGC 1275, and tidal forces inside the cluster have thoroughly disrupted it. Several filaments of newborn blue stars also cross the view.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded this view in visible light through blue, yellow-green and red filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures gather far more light than the eye can, which is what brings out faint structures like these filaments.

alt: A bright central galaxy surrounded by reddish, lacy filaments, with dark dust lanes and thin streaks of blue stars crossing the scene.

caption: The Hubble Ultra Deep Field, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Almost every speck in this picture is a galaxy, nearly 10,000 of them in many ages, sizes, shapes and colours. This is the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, described as the deepest visible-light image of the cosmos, a narrow core sample of the universe reaching across billions of light-years.

The nearest galaxies are the larger, well-defined spirals and ellipticals, seen as they were about 1 billion years ago. The smallest and reddest, around 100 of them, may be among the most distant known, glimpsed when the universe was only 800 million years old. In between is a zoo of oddballs. Some resemble toothpicks, others look like links in a bracelet, and a few appear to be interacting. They record a younger, more chaotic era when order was only starting to appear.

The patch of sky is tiny, just one-tenth the width of the full Moon, in the constellation Fornax, and from the ground it looks almost empty. Hubble needed 800 exposures over 400 orbits of Earth to build it.
explore: The total exposure time added up to 11.3 days. Looking into the field has been compared to peering through a soda straw 2.5 metres long, and the region is so empty of nearby stars that only a handful from our own Milky Way appear in the frame.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded this field in visible and near-infrared light. Blue and green show light the eye can see, such as from hot young stars and Sun-like stars, while red represents near-infrared light, such as the glow of dust-enshrouded galaxies.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light shown as red is invisible to the human eye, and ground-based photographs show this patch of sky as largely empty.

alt: A black field crowded with thousands of galaxies of different sizes, shapes and colours, from large spirals and ellipticals to tiny red specks.

caption: The Tadpole Galaxy (UGC 10214), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A spiral galaxy trails a long streamer of stars, like a pinwheel firework racing through space, in front of thousands of faint background galaxies. This is UGC 10214, nicknamed the Tadpole, which lies roughly 420 million light-years from us, in Draco.

A small interloper is to blame for the bent shape. It is the very blue, compact galaxy visible through the Tadpole's disc toward the upper left, likely a hit-and-run intruder that is now leaving. Gravity during the encounter pulled out the tail of stars and gas, which stretches more than 280 000 light-years. The collision also set off star birth. Blue clusters dot the arms and tail, each forming up to about a million stars, and two bright clumps in the tail, separated by a gap, will likely become dwarf galaxies orbiting the Tadpole.
Behind all this lies a wallpaper of about 3000 distant galaxies, twice as many as in the original Hubble Deep Field.
explore: The young clusters look blue because they contain very massive stars that are 10 times hotter than the Sun and shine 1 million times more brightly. As those stars burn out, the clusters grow redder and will eventually become old globular clusters like those around the Milky Way. This view took one-twelfth of the time spent on the Hubble Deep Field.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, installed during Servicing Mission 3B, built this colour image from three exposures through near-infrared, orange and blue filters. The exact colour assigned to each isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the faint background galaxies only show up because the camera collects light far longer than an eye can.

alt: A distorted spiral galaxy with a long tail of stars stretching to one side, a small blue galaxy in its upper left, set against many small distant galaxies.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1232, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Older, reddish stars fill the centre of this large spiral galaxy, while its arms are crowded with young blue stars and many regions where new stars are forming. This is NGC 1232, about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Eridanus, the River, photographed with ESO's Very Large Telescope and its FORS instrument.

Colour works as a rough clock for stars. The hottest, most massive stars shine blue but live only briefly, so blue light tends to mark places where stars formed recently. Older populations, which have lost their brightest members, glow redder, and that is why the core looks warmer in tone than the arms.

On the left side sits a distorted companion galaxy shaped like the Greek letter theta. Despite the great distance, the telescope's optical quality reveals a wealth of detail. The edge of the field corresponds to about 200,000 light-years, roughly twice the size of the Milky Way.
explore: The picture combines three exposures taken through ultraviolet, blue and red filters during a spell of good observing conditions, with north at the top. NGC 1232 lies 20 degrees south of the celestial equator.

understand.summary: ESO's Very Large Telescope with the FORS1 instrument made this from exposures in ultraviolet, blue and red light. The precise colour mapping for each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet light is invisible to the eye, and the camera's exposures gathered far more light than an eye could, revealing faint detail in the arms.

alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with a reddish centre and blue spiral arms, with a small distorted companion galaxy on the left.

caption: The Cigar Galaxy (Messier 82), imaged by the James Webb and Hubble Space Telescopes
story: Hourglass-shaped plumes of gas shoot out above and below a bright blue-white disc in this combined Webb and Hubble view. The disc is Messier 82, the Cigar Galaxy, an edge-on starburst galaxy about 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major.

In near-infrared light, Webb picked out the galaxy's swollen disc and, for the first time, millions of individual stars, roughly 16.5 million, which appear as tiny blue grains. Even so, astronomers think these are only a small share of the stars a galaxy like M82 contains.

The extreme star formation in M82 drives material out in two opposing plumes, a process that will eventually bring star birth there to a halt. Close to the disc, yellow tendrils mark ionised gas. Farther out, orange traces small dust grains called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which help astronomers follow the material between the stars, known as the interstellar medium.
explore: The scene has been evolving for a couple of hundred million years, so Webb's view is a snapshot in time. Its close look at the main plane of the disc is helping astronomers work out how M82 formed and what is happening inside it now. Distant galaxies appear in the background as small white and orange shapes.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam supplied near-infrared data and Hubble's ACS supplied visible light. Blue and cyan show shorter near-infrared wavelengths, yellow shows ionised gas seen by Hubble, orange traces PAH dust emission and red the longest near-infrared filter.
understand.eye: Most of this light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye. Only the yellow component comes from visible light.

alt: An edge-on bright blue-white galaxy disc with hourglass-shaped yellow and red plumes above and below it, a star with eight diffraction spikes to the right and small distant galaxies in the background.

caption: The Antennae Galaxies, imaged by ALMA and the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Red, pink and yellow clouds are laid over a blue visible-light picture of two colliding galaxies. These are the Antennae Galaxies, NGC 4038 and 4039, a pair of distorted spirals about 70 million light-years away in Corvus, the Crow. The blue comes from the Hubble Space Telescope and shows newborn stars, while the warmer colours come from ALMA.

ALMA picks up the clouds of dense, cold gas where new stars form, which visible light cannot show. It was tuned to pick up carbon monoxide molecules, which reveal otherwise invisible hydrogen clouds. Big concentrations of gas sit in the hearts of both galaxies and also in the chaotic zone where they collide. In the collision zone the gas adds up to billions of times the Sun's mass, a reservoir for future stars.
The ALMA data came from early testing, mostly with only twelve antennas placed close together. Even so, this was the best submillimetre-wavelength image ever taken of the pair.
explore: Longer wavelengths make sharp images harder to obtain, so here the Hubble picture remains the benchmark for resolution. Once the full ALMA array is completed, its vision is expected to be up to ten times sharper than Hubble's. Observations like these should help explain how galaxy collisions trigger the birth of new stars.

understand.summary: Visible light from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys appears mainly in blue, while ALMA's millimetre and submillimetre observations (bands 3 and 7) are shown in red, pink and yellow.
understand.eye: The cold gas traced by ALMA emits millimetre and submillimetre light that no eye can see.

alt: Two merging galaxies shown mainly in blue, overlaid with patches of red, pink and yellow marking cold gas clouds.

caption: The galaxy Centaurus A (NGC 5128), imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, Chile
story: This deep portrait shows the peculiar galaxy Centaurus A, also catalogued as NGC 5128, about 12 million light-years away in the constellation Centaurus. It was made with the Wide Field Imager, a camera mounted on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile.

The picture's depth comes from patience. Its exposures add up to more than 50 hours in total, which makes it probably the deepest view ever created of this unusual and spectacular object. Long exposures build up faint light that a short snapshot would miss, and that is how the dimmer outer parts of a galaxy can be traced.

Centaurus A is classed as an elliptical galaxy with an active nucleus. An active galactic nucleus is a compact galaxy centre that gives off far more energy than its stars alone would explain. Several of the filters used isolate the light of glowing oxygen and hydrogen gas.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope recorded visible light through several filters, including ones for oxygen and hydrogen-alpha emission. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: More than 50 hours of accumulated exposure gather far more light than the eye can, revealing faint structure no visual observer could see.

alt: A deep telescope image of the peculiar galaxy Centaurus A.

caption: The irregular galaxy Arp 263, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A broad band of tiny stars, denser on one side, is dotted with clumps of new stars wrapped in glowing blue gas, while plumes of red dust surround it. This is Arp 263, also catalogued as NGC 3239, an irregular galaxy about 25 million light-years away in Leo, seen by Webb's Near-Infrared Camera.

Arp 263 is believed to be the product of a past merger. It has two short, curved tails of stars, its stars are oriented differently from its hydrogen gas, and parts of that gas move at different speeds. Widespread star birth also hints that its gas has been badly stirred. The former partner, however, is nowhere to be found. It may have been a dwarf galaxy already dissolved, or one far heavier than it was bright.

Webb looks inside the thick gas to show older stars scattered through the galaxy beside busy nurseries. The most intense region features a curved chain of compact clusters leading to the brightest nebula.
explore: The brightest spot in the frame is a star in our own Milky Way, which is why it looks so large and has long diffraction spikes. Hundreds of far more distant galaxies show up behind it as orange dots. The data come from programme #3707, a survey of nearby star-forming galaxies in the southern sky. Halton Arp listed the galaxy in his 1966 atlas of peculiar galaxies.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed in near-infrared light. Blue and cyan mark shorter wavelengths including glowing hydrogen gas, green a water-ice filter, and red the glow of complex dust molecules (PAHs).
understand.eye: All of this light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye, and it lets Webb look inside the thick gas crowding the galaxy.

alt: A broad, irregular band of tiny stars with bright clumps wrapped in blue gas, red dust plumes, a large bright foreground star and a few background galaxies.

caption: The Antennae Galaxies, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Bright pink and red gas clouds surround flashes of blue star-forming regions, some partly hidden behind dark patches of dust. This is the Antennae Galaxies, NGC 4038 and NGC 4039, a colliding pair about 65 million light-years away in the constellation Corvus.

Both were once calm spirals like the Milky Way, but for the past few hundred million years they have been clashing. The encounter is violent enough to pull stars out of each galaxy into a streaming arc between them. Wider views show far-flung stars and gas stretching into long tidal tails, which give the pair its name.

The galaxies are in a starburst, a phase in which their gas is being turned into stars at a furious rate. It cannot last. Eventually the two cores will merge, and the pair will settle into retirement together as one large elliptical galaxy.
explore: Hubble had imaged the pair twice before, with WFPC2 in 1997 and with ACS in 2006. Each version improved on the last thanks to upgrades carried out during Hubble's servicing missions. This one combines Wide Field Camera 3 data with some earlier ACS observations.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys supplied visible and near-infrared observations. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared part of this light is invisible to the eye, and long exposures reveal far fainter gas and stars than an eye could see.

alt: Two merging galaxies with bright pink and red gas clouds, blue star-forming regions and dark patches of dust.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 2525, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble portrait shows NGC 2525, a barred spiral galaxy nearly 70 million light-years from Earth in the southern constellation Puppis. Together with Carina and Vela, Puppis makes up the image of the Argo, the ship from ancient Greek mythology.

A barred spiral has a straight band of stars across its centre, with the spiral arms reaching out from the ends. Like nearly every galaxy, NGC 2525 also hides a supermassive black hole at its core. Their masses can span from hundreds of thousands of Suns up to billions.

Hubble photographed this galaxy repeatedly for one of its major projects, which measures how fast the universe is expanding and can help answer fundamental questions about its very nature. From those observations, ESA/Hubble produced a time-lapse showing the galaxy together with a supernova slowly fading inside it.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed this galaxy in visible and near-infrared light. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, which is invisible to the human eye.

scaleExtra: NGC 2525 lies nearly 70 million light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Hubble.
alt: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 2525 seen by Hubble.

caption: The interacting galaxies Arp 142, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A distorted spiral nicknamed the Penguin and a compact oval galaxy called the Egg sit side by side, joined by a faint, upside-down U-shaped blue glow. Together they are Arp 142, about 326 million light-years away in Hydra, seen here in near- and mid-infrared light in a Webb image made to mark its second year of science.

The pair first swept past each other between 25 and 75 million years ago. That encounter unwound the Penguin's coiled arms, threw gas and dust in many directions and set off a wave of new stars, about 100 to 200 per year. The Milky Way, by comparison, makes roughly six to seven. Today the Penguin's centre resembles an eye, with star trails shaped like a beak, a backbone and a fanned tail.
Although the Penguin looks far bigger, the two have about the same mass, one reason they have not merged yet. The Egg holds old stars and little gas or dust, so it keeps its compact shape.
explore: The bright edge-on galaxy at top right, PGC 1237172, is not part of the encounter, since it lies 100 million light-years closer to us. It is young and not very dusty, so it nearly vanishes in Webb's mid-infrared view. Stars rarely collide when galaxies interact, but their orbits get disrupted. The Egg's stars are packed so tightly that it shows four diffraction spikes.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI combined near- and mid-infrared light. Blue and green show the shortest wavelengths, yellow and orange longer near-infrared light plus a mid-infrared PAH dust filter, and red a mix of the longest near-infrared filter and mid-infrared filters, including one for silicate dust.
understand.eye: Almost all of this light is infrared, which the human eye cannot see.

alt: Two interacting galaxies, a compact oval galaxy on the left and a distorted spiral on the right whose beak-like region points toward it, linked by a faint blue U-shaped glow, with many distant galaxies behind.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 5134, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A tilted spiral galaxy glows faintly blue with the light of its many stars, while bright red strands of dust swirl around a blue-white core and gather in places into orange clumps. This is NGC 5134, about 65 million light-years away in Virgo, captured by two of Webb's instruments working together.

The light in this picture left the galaxy soon after Tyrannosaurus rex went extinct, yet NGC 5134 counts as fairly close for a galaxy, so Webb can resolve fine detail in its tightly wound arms. The mid-infrared instrument, MIRI, traces warm dust in the gas clouds, some of it made of carbon-ring molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. The near-infrared camera, NIRCam, records light mostly from stars and star clusters.

Together they show a galaxy in constant give and take. Stars form in clouds along the arms, using up gas, and dying stars return some of it, either in supernova explosions or more gently as red giants shed their outer layers.
explore: Only stars above about eight times the Sun's mass end as supernovae, which can spread material across hundreds of light-years. The data come from observing programme #3707, which aims to study 55 nearby galaxies that are actively forming stars. Learning from close galaxies like this helps astronomers interpret distant ones, like the tiny background galaxies here that are barely more than points of light.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI combined near- and mid-infrared light. Blue, cyan and green show near-infrared starlight, orange traces PAH dust emission and red shows mid-infrared glow from warm dust.
understand.eye: All of these wavelengths are infrared and invisible to the human eye.

alt: A tilted spiral galaxy with a blue-white core and a faint blue disc, laced with swirling red dust strands and orange clumps, with tiny distant galaxies in the background.

caption: The galaxy Centaurus A, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A galaxy stretches horizontally across a field of tiny purple, pink and white points. Its brilliant white and pale pink centre throws out eight diffraction spikes, loops of pink and lavender arc above and below it in an S shape, and a grey and white band of dust cuts across the middle. This is Centaurus A, about 11 million light-years away, seen by Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument.
In visible light, thick lanes of dust hide much of this galaxy. Webb's infrared vision passes through them and reveals filaments, loops and glowing clouds of warm dust spread across the centre.

At the heart sits a supermassive black hole that is actively feeding and shines brightly. The tangled structures around it were shaped by a collision between galaxies in the past, and by activity that continues today. Farther out, the galaxy's edges fade into soft, feathery plumes reaching toward both sides of the frame.
explore: Mottled patches and bright knots are scattered along the dusty band. Around the galaxy, a few bright foreground stars show Webb's distinctive diffraction spikes, while countless fainter stars speckle the dark background.

understand.summary: Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument observed in mid-infrared light. Blue shows the shortest filter, cyan traces PAH dust emission and red a silicate-dust filter.
understand.eye: Mid-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it passes through dust lanes that block much of this galaxy in visible light.

alt: A horizontal galaxy with a bright white and pink centre with eight diffraction spikes, pink and lavender loops forming an S shape, and a grey-white dust band across the middle, on a background of tiny purple, pink and white points.

caption: The flocculent spiral galaxy NGC 2841, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble picture shows NGC 2841, a flocculent spiral galaxy about 65 million light-years away in the constellation Ursa Major. Instead of a few long, sharply defined arms, a flocculent spiral has short spiral arms, giving it a patchy, tufted look.

Star formation is one of the processes that most shape the universe. It plays a central part in how galaxies evolve, and it is during the earliest stages of a star's birth that planetary systems first appear. Even so, a lot remains unclear. Astronomers still ask how stellar nurseries change with the makeup and density of their gas, and what sets star formation going in the first place.

That second question is especially hard to answer for flocculent spirals like this one. Without long, prominent arms to point to, it is less obvious what drives new stars to form in galaxies such as NGC 2841.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed in ultraviolet, visible (including hydrogen-alpha) and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared parts of this light are invisible to the human eye.

alt: The flocculent spiral galaxy NGC 2841, with short spiral arms.

caption: The lensing galaxy cluster MACS J0454.1-0300, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Golden galaxies crowd the middle of this Webb picture, the largest and brightest at the centre, while heavily distorted orange galaxies curve around them in a great arc. The golden ones belong to the cluster MACS J0454.1-0300, seen at a time when the cosmos was around 8 billion years old. The orange ones lie much farther away.

Those distant galaxies look smeared because of gravitational lensing, in which the cluster's enormous mass bends and magnifies light from objects behind it. Even at the edges of the frame, small reddish galaxies have been bent into tiny arcs.

Lensing can also create several images of one galaxy. Four or more is rare, seen in only 10–20% of clusters, yet researchers found that arrangement twice here, the first time it has appeared more than once in the same cluster. The lensed images show a lone galaxy from only 800 million years after the Big Bang, and a merging group of galaxies from 2 billion years after it.
explore: Some bright knots in these lensed areas are magnified by a factor of more than 300. Compared with an earlier Hubble image of the same cluster, Webb reveals hundreds of galaxies that were always there but went unseen, because Webb is far more sensitive to their redder light. One programme behind the data will watch a lensed galaxy here for hugely magnified single stars.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed across near-infrared wavelengths, mapped from purple and blue for the shortest filters through cyan, green, yellow and orange to red for the longest.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Webb's sensitivity to red light reveals hundreds of galaxies missing from an earlier Hubble view.

scaleExtra: Some bright knots in the lensed galaxies correspond to regions as small as 5 light-years across, according to ESA/Webb.
alt: A galaxy cluster of golden elliptical galaxies with the brightest at the centre, surrounded by stretched orange galaxies forming an arc, plus a few bluish-white galaxies and stars.

caption: The spiral galaxy M74, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Bright pink patches are sprinkled along the spiral arms in this Hubble view of M74, a spiral galaxy about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Pisces, also known as the Phantom Galaxy.

Each pink patch is a huge cloud of hydrogen gas. Hot young stars embedded inside give off strong radiation that strips electrons from the hydrogen atoms, and the ionised gas glows in response. Astronomers call these star-forming regions HII regions, a label for hydrogen that has lost its electrons. They also show an excess of ultraviolet light, another sign of the hot stars inside.

HII regions make useful signposts. Because the clouds are relatively short-lived and are lit by young stars, they mark the places where a galaxy is forming stars in the present era rather than in the distant past.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue, visible, hydrogen-alpha and near-infrared filters. The full colour mapping isn't published, though the glowing hydrogen appears pink.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye can, and the near-infrared filter records light we cannot see.

alt: A spiral galaxy with bright pink patches of glowing gas dotted along its arms.

caption: A spiral arm of the galaxy M51, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Red-orange, clumpy filaments of gas and dust run in a chain from left to right, lit from within by glowing cyan bubbles that hold bright white star clusters. This is a stretch of one spiral arm in Messier 51, M51, seen by Webb's Near-Infrared Camera.

Stars are born in clusters when gas clouds collapse under gravity. As more stars form, stellar winds, harsh ultraviolet light and exploding massive stars eventually break the cloud apart. This is called stellar feedback, and it means most of the gas in a galaxy never ends up in stars.

M51 is one of four nearby galaxies studied in the FEAST programme. Astronomers identified nearly 9000 star clusters at different stages, from those just emerging from their birth clouds to those fully in the open. Webb looked inside the clouds while Hubble caught the unobstructed clusters, and together they showed that the most massive clusters clear away their gas fastest and begin lighting up their galaxy earliest.
explore: The red and orange colours represent infrared light from ionised gas, dust grains and complex molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Many of the stars strewn along the arm would be hidden from our eyes behind dust. Seeing inside the clouds let the team estimate each cluster's mass and age from its light.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed in near-infrared light. Blue marks the shorter wavelengths including a hydrogen line, green another hydrogen line, and red the glow of PAH molecules and the longest filter.
understand.eye: Many of the stars in this arm would be invisible to our eyes behind dust, but near-infrared light reveals them.

scaleExtra: The gas complexes along the arm are each tens or hundreds of light-years across, according to ESA/Webb.
alt: A long section of a galaxy's spiral arm made of red-orange clumpy gas and dust, with cyan bubbles and white star clusters inside, small stars throughout and a faint blue glow around the arm.

caption: The galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+2223, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Large blue spirals, pale white ellipticals and many orange and red galaxies fill this deep Webb view. This is the galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+2223, about 5 billion light-years away in Leo. More than 300 member galaxies have been confirmed, with several hundred more possible, and a huddle of ghostly ellipticals rules its centre.

The cluster's gravity bends light from galaxies behind it, an effect called gravitational lensing, stretching some into narrow streaks and twisting others into strange shapes. Just below the bright central galaxies, a spiral galaxy has been drawn out into something resembling a pink jellyfish. That galaxy hosts a star that once held the record as the farthest single star known, plus a supernova that showed up as four separate images simultaneously.
MACS J1149 was one of six clusters in Hubble's Frontier Fields programme, chosen because their strong lensing lets astronomers see into the early universe.
explore: Webb is now reaching even earlier times, turning up discoveries such as a supermassive black hole feeding heavily under 600 million years after the Big Bang. These data come from the CANUCS programme #1208, which studies low-mass galaxies in the early universe and the epoch of reionisation, when the earliest stars and galaxies began to shine.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed in near-infrared light, with the shortest filters shown in blue, middle ones in green and the longest in red.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the human eye.

alt: Many galaxies on a black background, including large blue spirals, pale white ellipticals, and numerous orange and red galaxies down to tiny faint spots.

caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 106, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope with amateur data
story: This view of Messier 106, also known as NGC 4258, blends Hubble observations with data from two amateur astronomers, Robert Gendler and Jay GaBany. It was Gendler who merged the Hubble data with his own observations to create the colour image. M106, a spiral galaxy, lies just over 20 million light-years away in the constellation Canes Venatici.

Pictures like this show that professional and amateur astronomy can work together. Observations gathered by dedicated amateurs on the ground were blended with data from a space telescope to produce a single colour portrait of the galaxy.
In astronomical terms, M106 is relatively nearby. Even so, the light captured here set out roughly 20 million years ago, so the galaxy appears as it was then rather than as it is today.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS, WFC3 and WFPC2 observed in visible and near-infrared light, including a hydrogen-alpha filter, and the result was combined with amateur ground-based data. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and combined datasets collect far more light than the eye can.

alt: The spiral galaxy Messier 106.

caption: The active galaxy Centaurus A, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, APEX and Chandra
story: Lobes and jets streaming from the centre of this galaxy are revealed in this composite, laid over its stars and its characteristic dust lane shown in close to true colour. This is Centaurus A, also known as NGC 5128, about 13 million light-years away, pictured by combining data from three instruments working at very different wavelengths.

Each layer shows something different. Visible light from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, Chile, captures the stars and the galaxy's characteristic dust lane. Submillimetre data at 870 microns, from the LABOCA camera on APEX, appear in orange. Data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, shown in blue, trace X-rays.

The lobes and jets stream out from the galaxy's central black hole, which is what makes Centaurus A an active galaxy. Only the visible-light layer shows the galaxy roughly as an eye would, while the orange and blue layers record light far outside the visible range.

understand.summary: Visible light from the Wide Field Imager shows stars and dust in close to true colour. Submillimetre data from LABOCA on APEX are shown in orange and Chandra X-rays in blue.
understand.eye: Submillimetre and X-ray light are both invisible to the eye, so only the visible-light layer resembles what an eye could perceive.

alt: A galaxy crossed by a dark dust lane, overlaid with orange submillimetre and blue X-ray data tracing lobes and jets from its centre.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1015, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Symmetrical arms swirl out from a bright central bulge in this face-on Hubble view, like a Catherine wheel firework. This is NGC 1015, a barred spiral galaxy about 118 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Cetus, the Whale.

The galaxy has a fairly large, bright centre, smooth and tightly wound arms, and a bar of stars and gas across the middle, much like our own Milky Way. Its arms curl outwards from a pale yellow ring around the bar. Bars appear in roughly two-thirds of all spiral galaxies. Scientists believe they may act as channels, funnelling gas and energy from the outer arms toward the core, where they could feed a central black hole, fuel star birth and build up the bulge.
In 2009, astronomers spotted a Type Ia supernova, SN 2009ig, in this galaxy. It shows up as one of the bright points above and to the right of the galaxy's core.
explore: Type Ia supernovae come from exploding white dwarfs that have companion stars, and they always reach the same peak brightness, 5 billion times that of the Sun. Comparing that known true brightness with how bright one appears gives astronomers a way to measure distances across the universe.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed this galaxy in visible and near-infrared light. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this data is near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and long exposures reveal far more than an eye could.

alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with symmetrical, tightly wound arms curling from a pale yellow ring around a bright central bar and bulge.

caption: The lensing galaxy cluster Abell S1063, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: An enormous bright-white elliptical galaxy sits at the heart of this Webb view, surrounded by other ellipticals and by short, curved, glowing red lines. The white galaxies make up the cluster Abell S1063, about 4.5 billion light-years away in Grus, the Crane. The red arcs are the main target, faint galaxies from the universe's distant past.

The cluster acts as a strong gravitational lens. Its mass is so great that light from galaxies lined up behind it bends around it, and like a glass lens it focuses that light, making the background galaxies brighter and larger, though distorted. Hubble's Frontier Fields programme had already used it as a magnifying glass on the early universe.

Webb pushes further back. This is a deep field, a long exposure of one patch of sky, built from 9 separate near-infrared snapshots adding up to around 120 hours. With the lens's help, it is Webb's deepest look at any single target so far.
explore: The data come from the GLIMPSE programme, which aims to probe Cosmic Dawn, the era of the first galaxies. The team has already found candidate galaxies from only 200 million years after the Big Bang, along with hints of the elusive first population of stars. A couple of foreground stars look big and bright, with long spikes.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed through nine near-infrared filters, mapped from purple and blue for the shortest wavelengths through green, yellow and orange to red for the longest.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and around 120 hours of observing collect far more light than any eye could.

alt: A huge bright-white elliptical galaxy at the centre of a cluster of ellipticals, ringed by short curved red arcs, with a couple of bright spiked foreground stars.

caption: The starburst galaxy Messier 82, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Tattered webs of cloud and flame-like plumes of glowing hydrogen burst out from the middle of this galaxy. This is Messier 82, M82, the starburst galaxy nicknamed the Cigar Galaxy, about 13 million light-years away in Ursa Major. The Hubble mosaic was described as the sharpest wide-angle view of M82 ever obtained.

The plumes rise from the galaxy's core regions, which are making young stars 10 times faster than our Milky Way does. That is what makes M82 a starburst galaxy, one that is forming stars at an unusually high rate during a phase of its history.

A mosaic stitches many separate pointings together, which is how Hubble, with its narrow but very sharp view, can cover a whole galaxy while keeping fine detail. One of the filters used isolates the light of glowing hydrogen, the gas that forms the flame-like plumes.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue, visible, hydrogen-alpha and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of hydrogen gas, and long exposures bring out plumes far too faint for the eye to see.

alt: An elongated galaxy with shredded clouds and flame-like plumes of glowing gas blasting out from its centre.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1672, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Clusters of hot young blue stars line the spiral arms of this galaxy, while clouds of hydrogen gas glow red and thin curtains of dust dim and redden the stars behind them. This is NGC 1672, a barred spiral about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Dorado, photographed by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

Its balanced, symmetric look comes from four principal arms, each edged by prominent dust lanes that reach out from the centre. A barred spiral has a straight band of stars across its middle, and the arms extend from its ends.

The colours trace star birth. Blue marks young, hot stars that formed recently, and the red glow comes from hydrogen gas in the regions where stars are being made. Dust makes starlight look redder as it passes through, because the grains scatter blue light more than red, so the dust lanes both hide and tint what lies behind them.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue, visible and red filters. The caption describes young stars as blue and hydrogen gas as red, but the per-filter colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures collect far more light than the eye can, revealing faint dust and gas.

alt: A symmetrical barred spiral galaxy with four main arms edged by dark dust lanes, dotted with blue star clusters and red glowing gas.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 2283, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Puffy, patchy clouds of gas and dust fill this close, nearly face-on view of a spiral galaxy, glowing red, orange and yellow and brightest at the centre and along two winding arms. This is NGC 2283, a barred spiral about 45 million light-years away in Canis Major, seen by Webb's NIRCam and MIRI.

Six snapshots through different near- and mid-infrared filters, adding up to 17 minutes, went into the picture. They show the galaxy's stars, hydrogen clouds heated by young stars, and sooty molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Dense knots of gas lit by young stars trace the arms, evidence that cold hydrogen is being turned into new stars.

Galaxies like this often host core-collapse supernovae. On 28 January 2023, one named SN 2023AXU was discovered here. Such explosions can fling gas across hundreds of light-years, enriching star-forming clouds with elements like oxygen and sodium that later end up in new stars.
explore: SN 2023AXU is a Type II supernova, which happens when a star with at least eight times the Sun's mass has its core collapse. The observations belong to programme #3707, which covers 55 nearby star-forming galaxies. The large, bright stars with diffraction spikes are in our own Milky Way, between us and NGC 2283.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI combined near- and mid-infrared light. Blue marks starlight and hydrogen emission, green and orange intermediate filters including PAH emission, and red the longest mid-infrared filters.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the human eye.

alt: A nearly face-on spiral galaxy full of patchy red, orange and yellow clouds of gas and dust, brightest at the centre and along two arms, with a few large bright white foreground stars.

caption: The starburst spiral galaxy NGC 1792, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: An orange glow spreads from the middle of this galaxy, while broad swathes of blue fill much of the rest of it. This is NGC 1792, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Columba, the Dove, in a close Hubble view.
The colours sort the stars by age. Blue marks areas full of young, hot stars, while the orange shades nearer the centre are where older, cooler stars reside.

NGC 1792 is also a starburst galaxy, forming stars at an unusually high rate. In such galaxies the pace can be more than 10 times that of the Milky Way. Galaxies with large reserves of gas, like this one, can have these short-lived phases set off by mergers or tidal interactions. You might expect a starburst to burn through all its gas in one go, but supernova explosions and strong stellar winds pump energy into the gas and scatter it, halting star formation before the fuel runs out. Scientists are still working to understand this balance.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The caption links blue to young hot stars and orange to older cooler stars, but the per-filter mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared parts of this light are invisible to the eye.

alt: A spiral galaxy with an orange glow at its centre and wide blue areas spread through its disc.

caption: The galaxy cluster MACS0416, imaged by the James Webb and Hubble Space Telescopes
story: Dozens of yellowish spiral and elliptical galaxies gather in the middle of this picture, surrounded by distorted streaks that seem to follow invisible circles around the centre, while red and blue galaxies crowd the rest of the field. This is the galaxy cluster MACS0416, about 4.3 billion light-years away, in a view combining Webb infrared data with Hubble visible light.

The light we see from the cluster left it shortly after our Solar System formed. Its gravity magnifies galaxies far behind it through gravitational lensing, creating those streaks, and the team has used it to spot supernovae and even single stars magnified enormously.

Colour here hints at distance. The bluest galaxies are relatively nearby and often forming stars intensely, which Hubble detects best. The redder ones tend to be farther away or very dusty, which Webb detects best. Together the two telescopes cover wavelengths from 0.4 to 5 microns.
explore: In general, the shortest wavelengths were coloured blue, the longest red, and those in between green. The result has been described as among the most colourful pictures of the universe yet made, and it holds details that could only be captured by combining both space telescopes.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS and WFC3 and Webb's NIRCam were combined. Blue shows Hubble's shortest wavelengths, green intermediate Hubble and Webb data, and red Webb's longest infrared wavelengths.
understand.eye: Much of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye. Only Hubble's shortest wavelengths fall in the range we can see.

alt: A cluster of dozens of yellowish galaxies at the centre, surrounded by curved, stretched streaks and many red and blue galaxies of various shapes on a black background.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2566, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A compact, pale core glows brightly at the centre of this oval spiral galaxy, filling its disc with bluish light, while faint reddish dust strands swirl outward and join arms of thick red dust with brighter orange patches. This is NGC 2566, about 76 million light-years away in Puppis, seen by Webb's NIRCam and MIRI.

The view shows the galaxy's well-defined arms, long central bar and fine web of gas, dust and stars. MIRI's mid-infrared data highlight warm dust, including sooty molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, while NIRCam reveals stars, even ones buried deep in gas clouds.

Being fairly nearby, NGC 2566 is a fine target for examining small-scale features such as star clusters and gas clouds. It is one of 55 galaxies in Webb programme #3707. Astronomers plan to combine these data with ALMA's view of the cold clouds where stars are born and with Hubble's census of young stars.
explore: ALMA uses 66 radio dishes to observe at the long-wavelength end of the spectrum. The Webb data belong to a Treasury programme, so scientists and the public can use them without a waiting period, letting exploration start straight away.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI combined near- and mid-infrared light. Blue shows starlight, green and yellow intermediate filters including PAH emission, and red mid-infrared glow from dust.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the human eye.

alt: An oval spiral galaxy with a bright pale core and bluish disc, with faint reddish dust strands joining thick red dusty arms with orange patches.

caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 5775, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the slender spiral galaxy NGC 5775 edge-on, so only a thin sliver of it is on view. That angle has an advantage, because the regions above and below the disc stand out far more clearly.

Astronomers have used this tilt to study a halo of hot gas around the galaxy that shows up at X-ray wavelengths. How such haloes form is unclear, but they surround spirals with high star formation rates like this one. Some astronomers think supernova explosions drive hot gas out of the disc into the halo, and it falls back as it cools, like an enormous galactic fountain.

NGC 5775 is also in the early stages of a merger. Bridges of hydrogen gas link it to NGC 5774, a nearby spiral seen face-on, yet neither galaxy has a tidal tail yet. Both belong to the Virgo Cluster, about 85 million light-years away.
explore: Tidal tails, disrupted streams of gas and stars reaching out into space, are common when two galaxies interact strongly, as in the Antennae Galaxies. NGC 5775 was imaged with the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, covering a field 3.2 arcminutes across.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded a red filter, shown here in blue, and a filter isolating the glow of hydrogen gas, shown in red.
understand.eye: The colours are assigned rather than natural, since red-filter light appears blue here, so the picture does not match what an eye would see.

alt: A thin, edge-on spiral galaxy seen as a slender sliver.

caption: The star-forming region Digel Cloud 2S, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A compact cluster of luminous red, blue and white stars sits at the centre, with faint, clumpy jets reaching out in several directions and a smaller cluster above and to the right. Translucent red wisps stretch across the scene. This is Digel Cloud 2S, a star-forming region in the Extreme Outer Galaxy, seen by Webb.

That region lies at the very outskirts of the Milky Way, over 58 000 light-years out from the centre of the Galaxy. To learn how a local environment affects star formation, scientists aimed Webb's NIRCam and MIRI at four star-forming areas in Digel Clouds 1 and 2, labelled 1A, 1B, 2N and 2S.

In Cloud 2S, Webb revealed a bright main cluster of newly formed stars, several of them shooting jets from their poles. The sub-cluster to its upper right had been suspected before and is now confirmed. Winds and radiation from nearby stars are carving away the red nebulous structures.
explore: Beyond the cloud lies a deep sea of background galaxies, appearing as small blue-white and orange-white dots and thin fuzzy discs. The larger blue-white point with diffraction spikes at upper right is a foreground star.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI combined near- and mid-infrared light. Blue and cyan show the shortest wavelengths, green and yellow intermediate ones, and orange and red the longest, including PAH dust emission.
understand.eye: This infrared light is invisible to the human eye.

alt: A compact cluster of red, blue and white stars with faint jets, a smaller cluster to the upper right, red wisps across the scene and scattered background galaxies.

caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 4183, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Seen edge-on against a backdrop of far-off galaxies and nearby stars, the spiral NGC 4183 shows off its disc, threaded with dark, intricate filaments of dust that block visible light from its core. It lies roughly 55 million light-years from the Sun in the northern constellation Canes Venatici, the Hunting Dogs, and belongs to the Ursa Major Group.

At about eighty thousand light-years across, it is a little smaller than the Milky Way. It has a faint core and an open spiral pattern, but from our viewing angle the arms are hard to appreciate. What we get instead is a clear look at the disc, which, like other galaxy discs, is built mostly of gas, dust and stars.

Recent studies suggest NGC 4183 may also have a bar. Bars are thought to funnel gas from the spiral arms toward the middle, boosting star formation there. Usually, new stars form more readily in the arms than in the central bulge.
explore: The British astronomer William Herschel was the first to observe NGC 4183. This picture combines visible and infrared images from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, covers a field about 3.4 arcminutes wide, and draws on data that Luca Limatola identified for Hubble's Hidden Treasures, a contest in image processing.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys (Wide Field Channel) combined visible and infrared images. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is infrared light, invisible to the eye, and long exposures reveal far more than an eye could.

alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy with dark, intricate dust filaments along its disc, set against distant galaxies and nearby stars.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2090, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Two curving, pale red spiral arms emerge from a shining central spot and each wraps once around this wide, oval galaxy, surrounded by a whirl of bright threads and dusty patches dotted with star formation. This is NGC 2090, about 40 million light-years away in Columba, in a combination of data from Webb's MIRI and NIRCam.

In visible light NGC 2090 looks flocculent, with a patchy, dusty disc and arms that seem flaky or vanish altogether. Webb's near-infrared camera brings those arms out clearly and also records starlight, shown in blue and strongest at the centre. MIRI picks up mid-infrared light, shown in red, given off mainly by carbon-based molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons along the strands of gas and dust.

Hubble studied this galaxy early in its mission, tracking Cepheid variable stars to help refine the Hubble constant. That 1998 study put the galaxy at 37 million light-years. Newer measurements place it slightly farther.
explore: NGC 2090 has long been a prominent nearby example of star formation. The Webb data come from programme #3707, a census of massive star-forming galaxies at just the right distance for Webb to capture their tight star clusters and the gas clouds where stars can be born.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI combined near- and mid-infrared light. Blue shows starlight, cyan and green intermediate filters, and red the mid-infrared glow of PAH molecules in the dust.
understand.eye: This infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it reveals spiral arms that look flaky or invisible in visible-light images.

alt: A wide oval spiral galaxy with a bright centre and two pale red arms each wrapping once around it, surrounded by bright threads and patches of dust, with foreground stars.

caption: The galaxy cluster Abell 2218, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble picture shows Abell 2218, a rich cluster made up of thousands of individual galaxies, about 2.1 billion light-years from Earth (redshift 0.17) in the northern constellation Draco. Scattered among the cluster's galaxies are long, thin arcs of light.

Those arcs are the work of gravity. The cluster's mass acts as a powerful gravitational lens, magnifying the images of galaxies hidden far behind it and letting astronomers look deep into the universe. The same effect also warps those background galaxies, stretching them into slender arcs.

Hubble's sharp vision means several of the arcs can be examined in detail. By comparing shapes and colours, astronomers can recognise when two or more warped images belong to one and the same background galaxy. Besides the big arcs, astronomers have also found many smaller arclets, each one a far more distant galaxy whose light has been bent on its way to us.

understand.summary: This view comes from the Hubble Space Telescope. The source doesn't list the instrument or filters, so the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures collect far more light than the eye can, revealing faint, distant galaxies.

alt: A rich cluster of galaxies with long, thin arcs of light scattered among them.

caption: The Sombrero Galaxy (Messier 104), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A brilliant white, bulging core sits inside thick dust lanes that trace the galaxy's spiral structure. This is the Sombrero Galaxy, Messier 104, named for its likeness to a broad-brimmed, high-crowned Mexican hat, shown here in a Hubble mosaic. From Earth it appears tilted nearly edge-on, and our view is only six degrees north of its equatorial plane.

The Sombrero lies about 30 million light-years away on the southern fringe of the rich Virgo galaxy cluster, where it ranks among the most massive members, equal to 800 billion suns. It spans 50,000 light-years.

With a fairly bright magnitude of +8, M104 sits just past the limit of what the naked eye can detect, though small telescopes show it easily. On the astronomical magnitude scale, smaller numbers mean brighter objects, so +8 sits just on the faint side of what unaided eyes can manage. Hubble's sharp view shows the core and dust lanes in detail.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The Sombrero is just beyond naked-eye visibility, so its dust lanes and glowing core only appear in detail through telescopes and long exposures.

alt: A nearly edge-on galaxy with a brilliant white, bulging core encircled by thick dark dust lanes.

caption: The interacting dwarf galaxies NGC 4490 and NGC 4485, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A large galaxy fills the left of this Webb picture, a smaller one glows white at the top right, and a bright red stream sweeps between them, dotted with concentrated patches of bright blue. The pair are the dwarf galaxies NGC 4490 and NGC 4485, together called Arp 269, about 24 million light-years away in Canes Venatici.

Leaving aside the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, which accompany our own galaxy, no interacting pair of dwarfs is known to be closer while showing both a gas bridge and individual stars that astronomers have directly observed. Dwarf galaxies probably resemble young galaxies in the early universe, being low in mass and in metals, rich in gas and home to relatively few stars.

About 200 million years ago the two swung close and then pulled apart. NGC 4490 captured a stream of gas from its partner, and the encounter sparked new stars along the bridge and in both galaxies. Another burst followed just 30 million years ago where their gas mixed.
explore: The blue patches are highly ionised gas around recently formed star clusters. A wispy gas bridge linking the galaxies was found nearly three decades ago. Webb's FEAST programme mapped where young, middle-aged and old stars sit, tracing the timeline of the encounter. One narrow-band Hubble filter was also used.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI were combined with one Hubble narrow-band filter. Blue shows short near-infrared wavelengths and Hubble's hydrogen filter, cyan and green intermediate ones, and orange and red the longest, including PAH emission.
understand.eye: Almost all of this light is infrared, which the human eye cannot see.

alt: Two interacting galaxies, a large one on the left and a smaller white-glowing one at top right, linked by a bright red stream with patches of bright blue, on a black background with distant galaxies.

caption: The centre of the Phantom Galaxy (M74), imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Delicate filaments of gas and dust trace the grand spiral arms that wind outward from the centre of this Webb view. This is the heart of M74, the Phantom Galaxy, around 32 million light-years away in Pisces, seen with Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument. With little gas in the nuclear region, Webb has a clear view of the star cluster at the very centre.

M74 is a grand design spiral, meaning its arms are prominent and well defined rather than patchy and ragged. It also lies almost face-on to Earth. Together, these traits make it a favourite for astronomers studying how spiral structure arises.

Webb observed M74 to learn about the earliest phases of star formation nearby, as part of the PHANGS collaboration's effort to chart 19 nearby star-forming galaxies in infrared light. Webb's longer wavelengths help pinpoint star-forming regions, gauge how massive and how old star clusters are, and study tiny grains of interstellar dust.
explore: Hubble had already revealed especially bright star-forming areas in M74 called HII regions. Hubble's sharp ultraviolet and visible view, Webb's infrared sensitivity and radio data from ALMA complement one another. MIRI was contributed by ESA and NASA and built by a European consortium working with JPL and the University of Arizona.

understand.summary: Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument observed in mid-infrared light, with the shortest filter shown in blue, then cyan and orange, and the longest in red.
understand.eye: Mid-infrared light is invisible to the human eye.

alt: The centre of a face-on spiral galaxy, with delicate filaments of gas and dust winding outward in spiral arms around a central star cluster.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 253, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, Chile
story: This wide view shows NGC 253, a nearly edge-on spiral galaxy in the constellation Sculptor, captured by the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla Observatory. The galaxy measures 70 000 light-years across and lies about 13 million light-years away.

Seeing a spiral close to edge-on means we look at its disc from the side, so the arms overlap along our line of sight instead of spreading out as a flat pinwheel. That angle hides some of the spiral pattern, but it shows how stars, gas and dust are layered through the thickness of the disc.

The picture was built from data taken through four filters, labelled R, V, H-alpha and OIII. The last two isolate light from hydrogen and from oxygen, elements that glow when gas in a galaxy is energised, so they help pick out the regions where that gas is lit up. The whole field of view spans 30 arcminutes.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager recorded visible light through R, V, hydrogen-alpha and oxygen (OIII) filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures gather far more light than the eye can, bringing out faint parts of the galaxy.

alt: A nearly edge-on spiral galaxy, NGC 253.

caption: The starburst galaxy Messier 82, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A blue-white disc runs from top to bottom through this image, while gas erupts from its bright centre forming an hourglass of red and orange dusty clouds on both sides. This is the central part of Messier 82, the Cigar Galaxy, just 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major, seen by Webb's NIRCam.

M82 is a smaller galaxy than ours, yet it shines five times as brightly and forms stars ten times faster. That pace is far quicker than expected for a galaxy of its mass, which is why it is classed as a starburst. In visible light, thick dusty clouds hide the central activity, but Webb's infrared view draws them back. Researchers suspect a gravitational encounter with a larger neighbouring spiral sent gas pouring into M82's centre millions of years ago, fuelling more than 100 super star clusters, each holding hundreds of thousands of stars.
The newborn stars in these clusters blast the surrounding gas with radiation and particles, launching the outflowing wind that Webb traces.
explore: Emission from PAH molecules outlines plumes only about 160 light-years wide, made of separate clouds 16–49 light-years across that appear to have been swept off the disc by the winds. An earlier Webb NIRCam image zoomed in on the very core, while this one takes a broader view of the centre.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed in near-infrared light. Blue and cyan show shorter wavelengths including iron emission, green molecular hydrogen, and orange and red PAH emission and the longest filter.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it passes through dust clouds that hide M82's centre in visible light.

alt: The centre of galaxy M82, a blue-white disc running top to bottom with an hourglass-shaped plume of red and orange dust erupting to the left and right, and distant galaxies behind.

caption: The peculiar galaxy NGC 3256, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble picture shows the peculiar galaxy NGC 3256, about 100 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Vela. Its distorted appearance is the legacy of a past galactic merger.

Mergers can stir up and compress the gas inside galaxies, and that can set off a starburst, a period of unusually intense star formation. Because its own merger has already happened, NGC 3256 is an ideal place to investigate starbursts that were triggered by galaxies coming together.

NGC 3256 was observed with two of Hubble's cameras, Wide Field Camera 3 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys, including filters that isolate light from glowing gas. An earlier Hubble image of NGC 3256 was released as part of a collection of interacting galaxies assembled for the telescope's 18th birthday, and this newer view revisits the same restless object.

understand.summary: Hubble's WFC3 and ACS observed in visible and near-infrared light, including filters for hydrogen and sulphur emission. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and filters tuned to glowing gas reveal detail the eye cannot see.

alt: The distorted peculiar galaxy NGC 3256.

caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 106, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A small, bright core floods the centre of this galaxy with bluish-white light, while broad swirling streaks of red and orange gas and dust mark its arms and two extra arms show up in green. This is Messier 106, also called NGC 4258, a spiral about 23 million light-years away in Canes Venatici, seen by Webb's NIRCam.

Like most spirals it has a supermassive black hole at its heart, but this one is unusually busy. The Milky Way's black hole only now and then draws in wisps of gas, while M106's is steadily consuming material, which heats up and radiates strongly as it spirals in. Webb observed it to study this active galactic nucleus.

The galaxy is known for two anomalous extra arms, seen in radio and X-rays rather than visible light and made of hot gas rather than stars. Astronomers believe the black hole's activity creates them, much like a wave bursting upward when it strikes a rock near the shore.
explore: Blue shows the spread of stars, orange warmer dust and deeper red colder dust, while teal, green and yellow near the centre trace gas. Despite the name, Charles Messier never catalogued it. His assistant Pierre Méchain discovered it, and it joined the catalogue only in the 20th century. Two supernovae have been seen in this galaxy.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed in near-infrared light. Blue shows stars, orange warmer dust, red colder dust, and teal, green and yellow trace gas near the centre.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the extra arms are normally detected in radio and X-rays rather than visible light.

alt: The central region of a spiral galaxy with a small bright bluish-white core, red and orange swirling arms of gas and dust, and two extra arms in green.

caption: The Sombrero galaxy, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A long blue disc stretches at an angle across a black background, with a small bright core at its centre. Its clearer inner disc is speckled with stars, while the outer disc looks whitish-blue and clumpy, like clouds in the sky. This is the Sombrero galaxy, about 30 million light-years away in Virgo, seen by Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument.
In mid-infrared light, the lumpy texture of the dust along the galaxy's outer ring comes into focus. That light picks out the gas and dust involved in forming stars in the outer disc.

The Sombrero is not an especially busy star factory, though. Its rings produce less than one solar mass of new stars each year, compared with roughly two for the Milky Way. Seeing the dust in such detail helps show where the modest star formation that does happen is taking place. Around the galaxy, distant galaxies appear as dots of different colours scattered across the dark background.

understand.summary: Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument observed in mid-infrared light. Blue and green show two PAH dust emission filters, and red the longest wavelength.
understand.eye: Mid-infrared light is invisible to the human eye.

alt: An oblong blue galaxy disc tilted across a black background, with a small bright core, a star-speckled inner disc and a clumpy whitish-blue outer disc, surrounded by distant galaxies.

caption: The star-forming ring of NGC 1097, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bright ring of star formation surrounds the core of NGC 1097, a barred spiral galaxy, in this Hubble image. The galaxy's larger structure is barely visible here, as its comparatively dim spiral arms loop loosely around the centre and reach beyond the frame. NGC 1097 is a face-on galaxy lying 45 million light-years away in the southern constellation Fornax, the Furnace.

It is a Seyfert galaxy. At its centre, a supermassive black hole 100 million times the Sun's mass is slowly drawing in the matter around it, and the region right beside it shines strongly with radiation from that infalling material. The ring, about 5000 light-years across, is packed with new stars, fed by material flowing toward the galaxy's central bar, and its star-forming regions glow with ionised hydrogen.
Supernova hunters like this galaxy too, since three supernovae went off in it in an 11-year span beginning in 1992.
explore: Outside this frame, NGC 1097 has two small companions. NGC 1097A is an elliptical orbiting 42 000 light-years from the centre, and NGC 1097B is a dwarf. Astronomers have signs that NGC 1097 and NGC 1097A interacted in the past. A version of this image was entered in Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition by Eedresha Sturdivant.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through a hydrogen-alpha filter and a near-infrared filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and the hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of ionised hydrogen.

alt: The centre of a barred spiral galaxy, with a bright ring of star-forming regions around its core.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 4945, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, Chile
story: Bright pink patches mark HII regions, places where stars are actively forming, across this edge-on galaxy. It is NGC 4945, about 13 million light-years away in the constellation Centaurus, the Centaur, pictured with the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla.

Observations suggest that NGC 4945 is a spiral resembling the Milky Way, with glowing, swirling arms and a central bar. Because we see it edge-on, though, those arms are not laid out flat before us as they would be in a face-on view.

One difference stands out. NGC 4945 has a brighter centre that likely hosts a supermassive black hole, thought to be swallowing large amounts of matter and hurling energy out into space. The image was assembled from five filter bands (B, V, R, H-alpha and S II), and the field of view measures 30 by 30 arcminutes.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope observed in five visible bands, including hydrogen-alpha and sulphur (S II) filters. Star-forming regions appear pink, but the full mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures gather much more light than the eye can.

alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy with a bright centre and bright pink star-forming regions along its disc.

caption: The galaxy cluster El Gordo (ACT-CL J0102-4915), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A blue overlay spreads across this crowded field of galaxies, mapping matter that cannot be seen directly. The galaxies belong to a cluster nicknamed El Gordo, or 'the fat one', about ten billion light-years away. No bigger cluster is known in the distant universe, and it holds several hundred galaxies.

New Hubble observations show it is some 43 percent heavier than earlier estimates, with a mass about three million billion times that of the Sun, or 3000 times the Milky Way's. Only a small part of that sits in the galaxies. More is in hot gas filling the cluster, but most is invisible dark matter, which the blue overlay traces.

Hubble weighed it through gravitational lensing, in which large lumps of mass bend space and skew our view of whatever lies behind them, revealing how much mass is doing the warping. Clusters this massive exist nearby, such as the Bullet Cluster, but none had been seen this early, when the universe was roughly half its present age (it is now 13.8 billion years old).
explore: An earlier study, in January 2012, weighed El Gordo using X-ray observations of the cluster's appearance and motions. Astronomers often name objects after distinctive features, such as the pinwheeling arms of the Whirlpool Galaxy or the long, thin silvery streak of the Needle Galaxy.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed in red and near-infrared light. The blue overlay maps dark matter, and the colour assigned to each filter isn't otherwise published.
understand.eye: Dark matter is invisible, and the blue overlay is a map derived from lensing measurements, not light an eye could see.

alt: A field of galaxies in the distant cluster El Gordo, with a blue overlay showing where the dark matter lies.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 5468, imaged by the Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes
story: A face-on spiral galaxy spreads four arms that curve outward counterclockwise, filled with young blue stars and peppered with small purplish star-forming regions. Its brighter, yellowish middle holds a distinct narrow bar. This is NGC 5468, about 130 million light-years from Earth, in a picture that merges Hubble and Webb data.

NGC 5468 is the most remote galaxy where Hubble has picked out Cepheid variable stars. These pulsating stars are mileposts for measuring how fast the universe is expanding, because the way they vary lets astronomers work out their true brightness, and so how far away they must be.

The distance derived from the Cepheids has been cross-checked against a Type Ia supernova in the same galaxy. Such supernovae are bright enough to measure distances far beyond the Cepheids' reach, carrying measurements of the expansion rate deeper into space. Galaxies that host both kinds of marker link the two steps together.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 supplied visible light shown in blue and green, and Webb's NIRCam supplied near-infrared light shown in red.
understand.eye: The red layer is near-infrared light that the eye cannot see.

alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with four blue arms dotted with purplish star-forming blobs, a bright yellowish centre with a narrow bar, and many red background galaxies.

caption: The dwarf galaxy DDO 82, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows DDO 82, also known as UGC 5692, a small galaxy that looks less like a grand spiral and more like a shapeless cloud of vapour. It lies about 13 million light-years away in Ursa Major, the Great Bear, and belongs to the M81 Group of around three dozen galaxies.

Few galaxies have the sweeping, glowing arms and bright centre of the Milky Way, and most look more like DDO 82. Tiny as they are, such dwarf galaxies still hold anywhere from a few million to a few billion stars.

DDO 82 is not entirely formless. Astronomers class it as a Magellanic spiral, named after the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf that orbits the Milky Way and is said to have a single spiral arm. In DDO 82, gravitational encounters over time seem to have scrambled that structure, so it is also described as a dwarf irregular galaxy.
explore: Its name comes from its number in the catalogue of the David Dunlap Observatory, a list of dwarf galaxies compiled by the Canadian astronomer Sidney van den Bergh. The image combines visible and infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and covers about 3.3 by 3.3 arcminutes.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed in visible and infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye.

alt: A small, shapeless dwarf galaxy resembling a faint cloud of stars.

caption: The galaxy NGC 7049, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Lacy webs of dust stand out in silhouette against the glow of millions of halo stars in NGC 7049, a galaxy in the southern constellation Indus about 100 million light-years away. Around the halo, a family of globular clusters shows up as glittering spots.

A globular cluster is a dense ball of old stars, and galaxies can have many of them orbiting in their outer halos. Because these clusters are so long-lived, they hold a record of their host galaxy's past, and astronomers study the ones around NGC 7049 to learn more about how it formed and evolved.
The dust, by contrast, is seen because it blocks light. With millions of halo stars shining from behind, the strands show up as a dark, lacy web laid across the glow.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue and near-infrared filters, with a synthetic green channel. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures bring out faint globular clusters and dust detail that the eye could not see.

alt: A galaxy with lacy dark dust lanes silhouetted against its bright halo, surrounded by small glittering globular clusters.

caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 77, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Streaks of red and blue pick out pockets of star formation along the pinwheeling arms of this galaxy, while dark dust lanes stretch across its starry centre. This is Messier 77, a spiral galaxy about 45 million light-years away in the constellation Cetus, photographed by Hubble.

M77 is a Seyfert galaxy, a class with an intensely active centre wrapped in highly ionised gas. Ionised gas has had electrons stripped from its atoms, which happens when it is bathed in strong radiation.

In this picture, the arms, star-forming pockets and dust lanes are the familiar features of a spiral. The Seyfert label instead describes the intense activity at the galaxy's very centre and the highly ionised gas around it. Hubble recorded the galaxy through visible, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha filters.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS and WFPC2 observed in visible, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha light. Beyond the red and blue streaks marking star formation, the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and the hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of hydrogen gas.

alt: A spiral galaxy with red and blue streaks along its arms and dark dust lanes across a bright starry centre.

caption: The interacting galaxies Arp 107, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A larger galaxy, just right of centre, has a hazy white core and a ring of red and orange gaseous filaments, with a noticeable gap at the top left edged by two big orange pockets of dust and gas. A smaller, hazy white galaxy sits beside it. This is Arp 107, a pair about 465 million light-years away, seen by Webb's NIRCam and MIRI.

The two galaxies collided hundreds of millions of years ago. In near-infrared light, shown in white, older stars shine brightly in both, along with a faint bridge of gas stretching between them. Background galaxies glow vividly at these wavelengths too.

MIRI's mid-infrared data show young stars and star-forming regions in orange and red, and give the clearest view of the point of impact, marked by the gap at the top of the spiral. The crash set off a fresh round of star birth and also produced what looks like a smile.
