understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam near-infrared data appear in white, and MIRI's mid-infrared data appear in orange and red.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the human eye.

alt: Two interacting galaxies, a larger one with a hazy white core and a ring of red and orange filaments with a gap at top left, and a smaller hazy white galaxy, among many distant galaxies.

caption: The giant elliptical galaxy NGC 1316 (Fornax A), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Surprisingly intricate loops and blobs of dust hide inside NGC 1316, a giant elliptical galaxy also known as Fornax A, about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Fornax. This Hubble image reveals its dust lanes and star clusters, tucked away like dust bunnies in the corners of a room.

That dust is a surprise. Elliptical galaxies are usually thought of as smooth collections of older stars, with little of the gas and dust that fill spiral galaxies. Finding such complex dust inside NGC 1316 therefore calls for an explanation.

The dust lanes and star clusters suggest one. They are evidence that the galaxy was built from a past merger of two gas-rich galaxies. The dust and clusters may be leftovers of that union, still visible long after the two became one.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and Hubble's sharp view reveal dust lanes and clusters invisible to the eye.

alt: A giant elliptical galaxy with complex dark loops and blobs of dust and scattered star clusters.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1559, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A pale glow fills this barred spiral galaxy, strongest along the bar that runs top to bottom through its core, while clouds of hot gas and dust crowd the centre and its loose, slightly ragged arms. This is NGC 1559, about 35 million light-years away in Reticulum, the Reticule, a southern constellation that gets little attention, seen by Webb.

Two instruments combine here. MIRI records the glow of dust grains that trace the interstellar medium, the raw material for future stars. NIRCam shows starlight, including young stars hidden behind thick dust, and the emission from ionised nebulae around them.

On the sky, NGC 1559 appears close to the Large Magellanic Cloud, but that is a trick of perspective. It is really a loner, with no galaxies nearby and no cluster to belong to. Its massive arms teem with star formation, and it is moving away from us at about 1300 kilometres per second.
explore: The data were gathered by the PHANGS team in a programme that will observe 55 galaxies also mapped by ALMA, Hubble and other facilities, aiming for a detailed picture of how stars are born, live and die. As a Treasury programme, its data have no exclusive access period, so anyone can use them at once.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI combined near- and mid-infrared light. Blue shows starlight and hydrogen emission, green and orange intermediate filters including PAH emission, and red the mid-infrared glow of dust.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the human eye.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy glowing pale along its vertical bar, with clouds of gas and dust around the centre and loosely wound, ragged arms containing a few bright star-forming regions.

caption: The edge-on disc galaxy NGC 5866, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A crisp dust lane splits this galaxy into two halves. NGC 5866 is a disc galaxy tilted nearly edge-on to our line of sight, about 45 million light-years away in the constellation Draco, seen here by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

The galaxy's anatomy is easy to read, with a subtle reddish bulge around a bright nucleus, a blue disc of stars running alongside the dust lane, and a see-through outer halo. Faint, wispy trails of dust wander away from the disc into the bulge and the inner halo. Hubble's sharp vision is what makes the dust lane look so crisp.

The outer halo is sprinkled with globular clusters, gravitationally bound groups of nearly a million stars each. Looking through the halo, Hubble also catches background galaxies that lie millions to billions of light-years beyond NGC 5866 itself.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue, visible and red filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal faint halo clusters and background galaxies that the eye couldn't see.

alt: A nearly edge-on disc galaxy split by a crisp dust lane, with a reddish bulge, a bright nucleus, a blue disc and a faint halo dotted with clusters and background galaxies.

caption: The dwarf starburst galaxy NGC 4449, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Countless stars fill this close view of a dwarf galaxy as tiny glowing points, brightest around its core, while thick clouds of gas and dust billow across the scene like curling flames, orange near the core and around bright clusters at lower left and dark red elsewhere. This is NGC 4449, also called Caldwell 21, about 12.5 million light-years away in Canes Venatici, seen by Webb.

NGC 4449 has been making stars for several billion years, but it is now doing so far faster than before, which makes it a starburst galaxy. At this pace its gas would run out in only another billion years or so. Unusually, the activity is widespread, with the youngest stars both in the nucleus and in streams around the galaxy. Encounters with a smaller companion, or with several neighbours, likely set it off.
Because it resembles primordial galaxies that grew by absorbing smaller systems, and is close enough to study in detail, it is an ideal laboratory for early galaxy evolution.
explore: Blue spots are individual stars, and a diffuse blue glow near the centre shows older stars. Yellow regions mark active stellar nurseries, orange-red traces PAH molecules, and bright red spots are hydrogen ionised by new stars. The galaxy belongs to the M94 group, close to our Local Group, and was observed in the FEAST programme.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI combined near- and mid-infrared light. Blue marks stars, yellow active stellar nurseries, orange-red PAH molecules and bright red spots ionised hydrogen.
understand.eye: This infrared light is invisible to the human eye.

alt: The centre of a dwarf galaxy full of tiny stars, brightest at its core, with flame-like clouds of gas and dust glowing orange near the core and bright clusters and dark red elsewhere.

caption: The spiral galaxy ESO 498-G5, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the spiral galaxy ESO 498-G5, about 100 million light-years away in the constellation Pyxis, the Compass. Its arms keep coiling right into the middle, so the core looks rather like a miniature spiral galaxy of its own.

Many spirals instead have a bright, elliptical central bulge that appears as a glowing mass. Astronomers call those classical bulges, and call spiral-like centres such as this one disc-type bulges, or pseudobulges. Hubble, free from the blurring of Earth's atmosphere, helped show that both types exist, and that stars are still forming in disc-type bulges while classical bulges have stopped.

The two also differ in how their stars move. Stars in classical bulges swarm on random orbits, like those in giant ellipticals, while disc-type bulges echo the orderly arms. That suggests different origins. Classical bulges are thought to grow through major events like mergers, and disc-type bulges slowly as stars and gas drift inward.
explore: Galaxies can be a bit like Russian nesting dolls. A classical bulge resembles a small elliptical galaxy set inside a spiral, while a disc-type bulge looks like a second spiral at the heart of the first. The image combines visible and infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, covering about 3.3 by 1.6 arcminutes.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye.

alt: A spiral galaxy whose arms wind all the way into its centre, making the core look like a small spiral.

caption: The Phantom Galaxy (M74), imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A large spiral galaxy fills the frame. Its mostly bright white core is circled by swirling structures that resemble water spiralling down a drain, and its rings glow deep red and orange, outlining filaments of dust around cavernous black bubbles. This is M74, the Phantom Galaxy, around 32 million light-years away in Pisces, revisited by Webb.

Dark red traces warm dust threading the galaxy, red shows light re-emitted by complex molecules forming on dust grains, and orange and yellow mark gas ionised by recently formed star clusters. Energy pouring from young stars, called stellar feedback, carves the network of bright knots and black bubbles. Little gas at the centre leaves a clear view of the nuclear star cluster.

The data come from the FEAST programme, which studies how feedback and star formation interact beyond the Milky Way. The team found that new stars slowly tear apart the gas and dust nurseries where they formed, and that star formation is most active in the spiral arms.
explore: M74 is a grand design spiral, with prominent, well-defined arms, and it lies almost face-on to Earth, a favourite combination for astronomers studying spiral structure. Webb also maps near-infrared hydrogen emission lines, which are less affected by dust and reveal where massive stars have just formed. ESA/Webb first featured M74 in August 2022.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI combined near- and mid-infrared light. Dark red and red trace warm dust and complex molecules, orange and yellow gas ionised by young clusters, and blue and cyan the shortest near-infrared wavelengths.
understand.eye: This infrared light is invisible to the human eye.

alt: A large spiral galaxy with a bright white core surrounded by swirling structures, and deep red and orange rings of dust filaments around dark bubbles.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 7331, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Arms swirl like a whirlpool around a bright central region in this Hubble view of NGC 7331, a spiral galaxy about 45 million light-years away in Pegasus, the Winged Horse, turned partly edge-on toward us. Near the yellow core, a tiny red dot marks a supernova that can still be faintly seen.

That supernova, SN2014C, is why Hubble observed the galaxy. In just one year it changed from an explosion with very little hydrogen into one rich in hydrogen. This rarely seen transformation was bright at high energies and sheds light on the poorly understood final stages of massive stars.

In many ways NGC 7331 resembles the Milky Way, being similar in size, shape and mass, with a comparable star formation rate, number of stars, central supermassive black hole and spiral arms. The main difference is that it has no bar of stars, gas and dust across its middle. Its central bulge also spins the opposite way to its disc.
explore: William Herschel first spotted NGC 7331 in 1784. Studying galaxies like it is a way of holding up a mirror to our own, helping astronomers understand parts of the Milky Way we cannot easily observe, as well as how galaxies behave and evolve in general.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed from ultraviolet through visible to near-infrared light, including a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared parts of this light are invisible to the eye.

alt: A partly edge-on spiral galaxy with swirling arms around a yellow core, with a tiny red dot near the centre.

caption: The MIRI Deep Imaging Survey field in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Thousands of galaxies of many shapes and sizes crowd a black background, most of them circles or ovals, a few spirals, the farthest shrunk to dots. This is part of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, revisited by Webb in the region known as the MIRI Deep Imaging Survey, or MIDIS.

Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument observed it through its three shortest-wavelength filters for nearly 100 hours in total, including Webb's longest look at an extragalactic field in a single filter so far. Combined with NIRCam data, the view turned up over 2500 sources in this small patch of sky, including hundreds of extremely red galaxies that may be massive and dust-shrouded, or mature systems whose stars formed early.

Colour tells astronomers about each galaxy. Orange and red ones give off extra long-wavelength light, from dust, heavy star formation or an active nucleus. Small greenish-white galaxies are especially distant. Most appear blue and cyan, brightest at shorter near-infrared wavelengths.
explore: Webb's sharp resolution, even in the mid-infrared, lets researchers make out the shapes of many of these galaxies and examine how their light is distributed, which helps explain how they grew. The MIRI observations were part of Webb programmes #1283 and #6511.

understand.summary: Webb's MIRI and NIRCam data are combined. Blue and cyan show near-infrared light, white and green the peak mid-infrared wavelengths, and orange and red the longest mid-infrared wavelengths.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the human eye.

alt: A deep field of thousands of galaxies on black, mostly small circles and ovals with a few spirals, some glowing red and orange.

caption: Globular clusters in the core of the Coma Cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thousands of tiny dots scattered through this Hubble view are globular clusters at the core of the Coma cluster. Coma is an enormous, gravitationally bound family of over 1000 galaxies, roughly 320 million light-years from us. The picture comes from a survey that pooled data from three of Hubble's observing programmes.

Astronomers counted over 22 000 globular clusters, some forming a bridge between NGC 4889 and NGC 4874, a famous interacting pair. Normally, a globular cluster is a ball of stars orbiting one galaxy as a satellite, but these are intracluster globular clusters, bound to the galaxy cluster as a whole rather than to any single galaxy.

At this distance they look like mere dots even to Hubble. Colour is the key. Stars in a cluster formed at about the same time from the same material, so each cluster has a consistent colour. By analysing colour and size, astronomers picked out the clusters and ruled out background galaxies.
explore: The clusters help map how matter, and especially dark matter, is spread through Coma. Coma was among the earliest places where odd gravitational behaviour pointed to the existence of dark matter.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures show thousands of faint clusters far beyond the reach of the eye.

alt: A field dotted with thousands of tiny points of light, globular clusters, at the core of the Coma galaxy cluster.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 7714, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Strangely shaped arms and a smoky golden haze stretching from the centre give NGC 7714 an unsettled look in this Hubble image. This spiral lies 100 million light-years from Earth, in the constellation Pisces, a fairly close neighbour by cosmic standards.

Those distortions are signs of violent events in the galaxy's recent past. NGC 7714 is in the midst of an ongoing merger with a smaller companion galaxy, NGC 7715, which lies outside the frame, and that encounter is behind both the odd arms and the golden haze.

Mergers are a common way for galaxies to change over time. As two galaxies pass close, their mutual gravity tugs on stars and gas, reshaping both, and over long periods they can combine into one. NGC 7714 gives a relatively nearby view of that process while it is still under way.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared parts of this light are invisible to the eye.

alt: A spiral galaxy with oddly shaped arms and a golden haze extending from its centre.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 24, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Blue bursts of young stars, dark lanes of dust and red bubbles of hydrogen gas pepper the spiral arms of NGC 24, with distant galaxies hovering around its edge. The galaxy lies about 25 million light-years away in Sculptor and measures some 40 000 light-years across, seen here by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

Astronomers suspect that spirals like NGC 24 and the Milky Way sit inside extended haloes of dark matter, a mysterious substance that cannot be seen and reveals itself only through its gravitational pull on surrounding material. About 80% of NGC 24's mass is thought to lie in such a halo.

Dark matter was originally suggested because the outer regions of galaxies, including ours, spin surprisingly quickly. It is also thought to play an essential part in how galaxies form and evolve. The galaxy itself was discovered by the British astronomer William Herschel in 1785.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed in visible and near-infrared light. The caption links blue to young stars and red to hydrogen gas, but the per-filter mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Dark matter can't be seen at all, and the near-infrared light here is also invisible to the eye.

alt: A spiral galaxy disc with blue patches of young stars, dark dust lanes and red bubbles of gas, surrounded by small distant galaxies.

caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 100, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble portrait shows Messier 100, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Coma Berenices, taken with Wide Field Camera 3. Hubble has photographed this galaxy before, most famously in a pair of pictures made about a month apart, one before and one after the telescope's first servicing mission, flown in December a quarter of a century before this image was released.

Soon after launch, Hubble's pictures came back fuzzy, as though out of focus. Its main mirror, which works like a satellite dish gathering light to one focal point, had a flaw called spherical aberration, in which light hitting the mirror's rim did not meet at the same point as light from its middle.

Seven astronauts fixed this on that first servicing mission by fitting a device named COSTAR, which compensated for the flaw so the instruments could sharpen their images. The before-and-after pictures of M100 showed a big jump in quality. COSTAR stayed on board until Servicing Mission 4, and every later instrument had corrective optics built in.
explore: COSTAR stands for Corrective Optics Space Telescope Axial Replacement. By the time it was removed, all of Hubble's original instruments had been swapped out. The newer M100 portrait shows how far the current generation of cameras has come compared with those Hubble carried at launch and just after the first repair.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal much more of the galaxy's faint structure than an eye could see.

alt: The spiral galaxy Messier 100.

caption: The merging galaxies NGC 1512 and NGC 1510, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1512 sits on the left of this Hubble composite, with the dwarf galaxy NGC 1510 on the right. It was stitched together from two separate Hubble pointings, and both galaxies lie about 30 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Horologium.

The pair are in the middle of merging. When the process is complete, the larger NGC 1512 will have cannibalised its small companion, taking its stars and gas into itself. Mergers in which a big galaxy swallows a much smaller one are one of the ways galaxies grow over time.

A barred spiral like NGC 1512 has a straight band of stars across its centre, with its arms extending from the bar's ends. A dwarf galaxy is a small system holding far fewer stars than a large spiral. Hubble has caught the two while they are still separate, before the smaller one disappears into its neighbour.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared parts of this light are invisible to the eye.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy on the left and a small dwarf galaxy on the right.

caption: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: More than 100 million stars, along with thousands of star clusters, crowd this Hubble view of the Andromeda galaxy, also known as M31. It covers a section of the galaxy's flat, pancake-shaped disc reaching across more than 40 000 light-years.

The full image was the largest and sharpest ever made of Andromeda, and the biggest Hubble image ever released. Even this cropped version holds 1.5 billion pixels. Showing the whole picture at full resolution would take more than 600 HD television screens, so it is best explored with a zoom tool.

Andromeda is a spiral galaxy about 2 million light-years away, in the constellation that shares its name. Because it is so close, Hubble can separate individual stars across a whole stretch of its disc, rather than just the blended glow seen in more distant galaxies. That is how a single picture can show more than 100 million stars.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through a blue filter and a near-infrared filter. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light we cannot see, and Hubble separates stars that would blur together for the eye.

alt: A dense field of millions of stars and star clusters in a section of the Andromeda galaxy's disc.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 4394, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Bright spiral arms, sprinkled with young blue stars, dark filaments of dust and fuzzy patches of star formation, spring from the ends of a bar that crosses the central bulge of NGC 4394. This barred spiral lies about 55 million light-years from Earth in Coma Berenices, Berenice's Hair, and is counted as part of the Virgo Cluster.

It is the textbook example of a barred spiral. At its centre sits a region of ionised gas called a LINER, whose spectrum shows a telltale set of emission lines, mostly from weakly ionised oxygen, nitrogen and sulphur.

LINERs are fairly common, but what powers them is still unclear. In most cases a central black hole is thought to be responsible, although lots of star formation could also do it. In NGC 4394, gravitational interaction with a neighbour has likely pushed gas into the centre, giving fresh fuel either to the black hole or to new stars.
explore: The German–British astronomer William Herschel discovered NGC 4394 in 1784. The picture draws on data from more than one of Hubble's cameras, and the image credit acknowledges Judy Schmidt.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS and WFPC2 observed in blue and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and near-infrared light reveal detail beyond the reach of the eye.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy whose bright arms, dotted with blue stars, dark dust and fuzzy star-forming patches, spring from the ends of a central bar.

caption: The flocculent spiral galaxy NGC 2775, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Delicate, feathery spiral arms, full of millions of bright young blue stars and laced with dark lanes of dust, surround a large central bulge in this Hubble image. This is NGC 2775, a flocculent spiral galaxy about 67 million light-years away in the constellation Cancer.

Those soft, patchy arms suggest the galaxy's recent star formation has been fairly calm. Its middle has almost no new stars at all, being dominated by an unusually large bulge with little in it, where all the gas was used up making stars long ago.

Groups of hot blue stars are thought to set off star formation in nearby gas clouds, and as the galaxy turns, those clouds are sheared out, which is thought to produce the feathery pattern. Flocculent spirals like this contrast with grand design spirals, whose arms are prominent and sharply defined.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed from ultraviolet through visible to near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared parts of this light are invisible to the eye.

alt: A spiral galaxy with a large central bulge surrounded by feathery arms of blue stars and dark dust lanes.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy M83, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Two spiral arms reach sideways from a barred galaxy's core and merge into a broad network of gas and dust that fills the frame, glowing bright orange along the arms and darker red elsewhere. Through gaps in the dust, countless tiny stars show, packed most densely around the core. This is M83, also known as NGC 5236, about 15 million light-years away in Hydra, seen by Webb's MIRI.

MIRI observes mid-infrared light between 5 and 28 micrometres, far beyond the roughly 0.38 to 0.75 micrometres our eyes respond to. It doesn't take in that whole range at once. It has ten filters, each passing a narrow slice. This image uses just two, near the short end.

Bright blue shows stars across the central galaxy, yellow marks active stellar nurseries threading the arms, and orange-red traces carbon-based molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which one of the two filters is especially good at imaging.
explore: M83 was observed in the FEAST programme, whose six galaxies, M51 among them, were all imaged with both NIRCam and MIRI, two of Webb's four instruments. As an example of how narrow the filters are, F770W passes only light between 6.581 and 8.687 micrometres.

understand.summary: Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument used two filters. Blue shows stars, yellow stellar nurseries and orange-red PAH molecules.
understand.eye: Mid-infrared light lies well outside the range the human eye can see.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy with two arms reaching sideways into a network of orange and dark red gas and dust, with countless tiny stars visible through the gaps, densest at the core.

caption: The dwarf galaxy I Zwicky 18, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A dwarf irregular galaxy dominates this Webb view, its core a bright region of white and blue stars split into two distinct lobes and wrapped in brown, dusty filaments. Small galaxies, white ovals and red spirals, are scattered across the black background. This is I Zwicky 18, roughly 59 million light-years from Earth.

Star formation in this galaxy has come in several sudden bursts, and two major starburst regions sit in its heart. The brown filaments are bubbles of gas heated by winds and fierce ultraviolet light from hot young stars. Webb's data suggest the two regions peaked at different times, with the strongest activity more recent in the northwest lobe than in the southeast one.

I Zw 18 has one of the lowest shares of elements heavier than helium of any galaxy in the local universe, conditions thought similar to some of the first star-forming galaxies. Studying it should therefore help reveal how stars and dust behaved in the early universe.
explore: Once thought to be forming its very first stars, it turned out to hold fainter, older red stars seen by Hubble, suggesting star formation began at least one billion and possibly 10 billion years ago. A nearby companion galaxy may be interacting with it and could have set off its recent star formation. Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky first identified it in the 1930s.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed in near-infrared light. Blue and cyan show the shorter wavelengths, orange and red the longer ones.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the human eye.

alt: A dwarf irregular galaxy with a bright two-lobed core of white and blue stars surrounded by brown dusty filaments, among small white and red background galaxies.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 3717, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble picture shows the spiral galaxy NGC 3717 almost side-on, about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Hydra, the Sea Serpent.

Seeing a spiral nearly in profile shows its three-dimensional shape clearly. Across most of their extent, spiral galaxies are thin, like a pancake. At their cores, though, they have bright, rounded, star-packed bulges that rise above and below the disc, so from the side they look a little like a flying saucer.

NGC 3717 is not quite perfectly edge-on. Its nearer part tips very slightly down and its far side slightly up. That angle gives a view across both the disc and the central bulge, although only one side of the bulge can be seen. Hubble sees galaxies at every kind of orientation, and sideways views like this one are especially good at conveying depth.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye.

alt: A spiral galaxy seen almost edge-on, with a thin disc and a bright central bulge visible on one side.

caption: The elliptical galaxy Messier 59 (NGC 4621), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A glowing, rounded ball of light fills this Hubble image. It is the galaxy NGC 4621, more familiar as Messier 59, photographed with the Advanced Camera for Surveys. It lies about 50 million light-years away in the Virgo Cluster, a gathering of some 2000 galaxies in the constellation Virgo, the Virgin.

Modern observations show Messier 59 is an elliptical, one of the three main kinds of galaxy alongside spirals and irregulars. Ellipticals are usually the most mature of the three, full of old red stars and forming few or no new ones.

Messier 59 partly breaks that pattern. It shows signs of star formation, with some newborn stars living in a disc close to its core. Finding young stars there shows that even galaxies dominated by old stars can still hold pockets of fresh activity.
explore: The French comet hunter Charles Messier added the galaxy to his famous catalogue of deep-sky objects, which is where its better-known name comes from. However, credit for its discovery goes to the German astronomer Johann Gottfried Koehler, who found it just days before Messier listed it.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS and WFPC2 observed in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal far more of the galaxy's glow than an eye could.

scaleExtra: Messier 59 lies approximately 50 million light-years away, according to ESA/Hubble.
alt: A bright, rounded elliptical galaxy.

caption: The lensing galaxy cluster SDSS J1226+2152, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A cluster of galaxies, most oval and smooth, a few with spiral arms, fills this Webb image. The largest sits in the centre, and near it several background galaxies have been stretched and warped into long arcs. The cluster is SDSS J1226+2152 in Coma Berenices, and every one of the tiny pinpricks is a galaxy rather than a star.

The arcs are gravitational lensing. The cluster's mass warps spacetime and bends light from galaxies far behind it, as if a giant lens were redirecting it, magnifying those galaxies as well as distorting them. The innermost lensed galaxy, just above and right of the central one, is SGAS J122651.3+215220, seen roughly two billion years after the Big Bang.
Lensing combined with Webb's power should let astronomers measure where and how fast stars are forming in that galaxy, and what kinds of environment support it.
explore: Many of the paler white galaxies probably belong to cosmic noon, an era of intense star birth between two and three billion years into cosmic history, while the few small orange and red ones likely come from even earlier. The picture was among Webb's early science observations.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed in near-infrared light. Blue shows the shortest wavelengths, green intermediate ones and red the longest.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the human eye.

alt: A galaxy cluster of mostly smooth oval galaxies with a large one at the centre, surrounded by stretched arcs of background galaxies, on a black background full of tiny galaxies.

caption: The galaxy UGCA 193, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Looking rather like a waterfall, this galaxy seems to hold many young stars, especially in its lower part, which gives it a blue haze and the impression that stars are tumbling down from above. It is UGCA 193, a galaxy in the constellation Sextans, the Sextant, photographed by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.
That blue colour tells us the stars on view are hot, some with temperatures more than 6 times the Sun's. To our eyes, cooler stars look redder and hotter stars look bluer.

A star's mass, surface temperature and colour are all linked. Heavier stars burn at higher temperatures, so their surfaces glow blue. Massive blue stars also use up their fuel relatively quickly, which is why a strong blue glow like this one generally points to a population of young stars, recently formed in the galaxy.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published, though the caption links the blue haze to hot young stars.
understand.eye: Part of this light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye.

alt: A galaxy with a blue haze of young stars concentrated in its lower portion, resembling a waterfall.

caption: The spiral galaxies NGC 2207 and IC 2163, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two spiral galaxies slip past each other like great ships in the night in this Hubble image, taken with the Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. They are NGC 2207 and IC 2163, about 110 million light-years away in the direction of the constellation Canis Major.

The pair are caught in a near-collision, a grazing encounter rather than a head-on crash. When galaxies come this close, each one's gravity pulls on the other's stars and gas, and over time such encounters can reshape both of them.

A spiral galaxy is a flattened disc of stars, gas and dust with arms winding out from a central region. NGC 2207 and IC 2163 are caught at a single moment in an interaction that unfolds over spans of time far longer than a human life, so one image cannot show the motion itself.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 observed from ultraviolet through visible to near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared parts of this light are invisible to the eye.

alt: Two spiral galaxies side by side in a near-collision.

caption: The irregular galaxy IC 10, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows IC 10, an irregular galaxy in the Local Group, the family of over 50 galaxies in our galactic neighbourhood that includes the Milky Way. It lies about 2.2 million light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia.

IC 10 is the closest known starburst galaxy, meaning it is forming stars at a furious pace, fed by plentiful cool hydrogen. That gas gathers into vast molecular clouds, which then break into dense knots. When pressure and temperature in a knot climb high enough, nuclear fusion switches on and a new star is born.

As an irregular galaxy, it has neither the grand shape of a spiral nor the smooth, rounded look of an elliptical. It is also faint for such a close galaxy, and was only discovered in 1887, by the American astronomer Lewis Swift. It stays hard to study because our line of sight to it is crowded with dust and stars.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Dust along our line of sight dims IC 10, and long exposures reveal far more than the eye could.

alt: The irregular galaxy IC 10, without a clear spiral or rounded shape.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2008, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The spiral galaxy NGC 2008 takes centre stage in this Hubble image, its ghostly arms spreading out toward us. It lies roughly 425 million light-years away in the constellation Pictor, the Painter's Easel.

Discovered by John Herschel in 1834, NGC 2008 is classed as type Sc in the Hubble sequence, a system for sorting galaxies by shape. The S marks it as a spiral, and the c means it has a fairly small central bulge and more open arms. Spirals with bigger bulges tend to have more tightly wound arms and are classed Sa, with type Sb in between.

Spirals are everywhere, making up over 70% of all observed galaxies, the Milky Way among them. Being common doesn't make them any less beautiful. These huge, whirling collections of billions of stars rank among the most memorable sights that telescopes like Hubble have recorded.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye.

alt: A spiral galaxy at centre with faint, ghostly arms spreading outward.

caption: The Sombrero Galaxy (Messier 104), imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A dominant bulge of mature stars glows behind a nearly edge-on disc of stars, gas and intricately structured dust, which shows up as dark lanes across the galaxy and most clearly right in front of the bright nucleus. This is Messier 104, the Sombrero, named for its Mexican-hat shape, about 50 million light-years away in Virgo, imaged with ESO's Very Large Telescope.

A swarm of small, slightly fuzzy objects fills the galaxy's halo. Most are globular clusters, like those around our own Galaxy. Despite the massive bulge, a sizeable part of the disc can be seen on its far side too.

M104 is the 104th object in Charles Messier's famous catalogue of nebulae. It was missing from the first two editions, but Messier soon added it by hand to his own copy as a 'very faint nebula'. In 1912 Vesto M. Slipher at Lowell Observatory first measured how fast it is receding, about 1000 km/sec, and was also first to detect its rotation.
explore: The image combines three exposures from the FORS1 instrument on the VLT's ANTU telescope, taken through V, R and I bands and rendered as blue, green and red. The seeing, a measure of how much the atmosphere blurred the view, was 0.6–0.7 arcseconds.

understand.summary: FORS1 on the VLT's ANTU unit recorded V-band light (shown blue), R-band light (green) and near-infrared I-band light (red).
understand.eye: The I-band light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye, and the long exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

alt: A nearly edge-on galaxy with a large glowing bulge, dark dust lanes across its disc and a swarm of faint globular clusters around it.

caption: The radio galaxy Centaurus A, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Thick layers of dust almost completely hide the centre of Centaurus A, also known as NGC 5128, in this image from the FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope. Many massive, luminous blue stars are resolved individually, notably toward the upper right and lower left. The galaxy lies roughly 10 to 13 million light-years away.

Among galaxies with a radio-loud active nucleus, Centaurus A is a leading example. Sir John Herschel was the first to report its dusty structure, and until 1949 it was thought to be an odd object inside the Milky Way, before being recognised as a powerful radio galaxy. Its core is the smallest known radio source beyond our galaxy, only 10 light-days across, and probably holds a supermassive black hole of about 100 million solar masses.

There is strong evidence that it formed from a merger of an elliptical and a spiral galaxy, because an elliptical alone would not have held the dust and gas needed to make the young blue stars lining the dust lane.
explore: It is one of the most thoroughly studied objects in the southern sky, observed at every wavelength from radio to gamma rays. A jet of high-energy particles from the centre shows up in radio and X-ray images. Its apparent visual magnitude is about 8, so it cannot be seen without optical aid.

understand.summary: FORS2 on the Very Large Telescope recorded blue (B), green-yellow (V) and red (R) exposures, shown as blue, green and red.
understand.eye: At about magnitude 8, Centaurus A is too faint for the unaided eye, and long exposures reveal its dust and individual stars.

alt: A galaxy whose centre is almost hidden by thick dust layers, with many blue stars resolved around it.

caption: The spiral galaxy M81, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble photo shows the spiral galaxy M81, about 11 million light-years away in the constellation Ursa Major. It was recorded with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue, visible and near-infrared filters.

Somewhere within it lies supernova 1993J. Astronomers found that this exploded star had a companion star that had stayed hidden in the supernova's glare for 21 years. An annotated version of the image marks the spot where the supernova sits.

A supernova is the explosive death of a star, bright enough for a while to be seen across intergalactic distances. Its glow can easily outshine a neighbouring star, which is how the companion of supernova 1993J could stay hidden for so long before astronomers finally picked it out.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and near-infrared light reveal detail the eye can't see.

alt: The spiral galaxy M81.

caption: The interacting galaxies NGC 6872 and IC 4970, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A huge barred spiral shaped like an integral sign stretches diagonally across this image, with a smaller interacting galaxy just above the centre. The large galaxy is NGC 6872 and its companion is IC 4970, a system almost 300 million light-years away in the southern constellation Pavo, the Peacock, imaged with FORS1 on ESO's Very Large Telescope.

From tip to tip NGC 6872 spans nearly 750,000 light-years, making it one of the largest known barred spirals. Its upper left arm is noticeably disturbed and crowded with bluish objects, many of them star-forming regions. That may be the result of IC 4970 recently passing through it.

To fit the whole galaxy into the camera's field, the instrument was rotated so the galaxy lies along the diagonal. The bright object at lower right is a star in the Milky Way, badly overexposed and showing multiple reflections within the telescope and instrument.
explore: Many fainter, more distant galaxies of varied shapes also fill the field. NGC 6872 is classified as type SBb and IC 4970 as type S0. The colour picture was assembled from blue, green-yellow and red exposures taken with the VLT's ANTU unit.

understand.summary: FORS1 on the VLT's ANTU unit combined blue (B), green-yellow (V) and red (R) exposures into a three-colour composite.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal the faint outer arms and distant galaxies beyond the reach of the eye.

alt: A long barred spiral galaxy shaped like an integral sign across the frame, a small companion galaxy near the centre, and a bright overexposed star at lower right.

caption: The central region of the spiral galaxy Messier 83, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This view shows the central region of Messier 83, a spiral galaxy also known as NGC 5236, about 15 million light-years away in the southern constellation Hydra, the Water-Snake. It was made with the FORS1 instrument on the VLT's ANTU telescope by overlaying three frames taken through different filters.
Its spiral pattern resembles that of our own Milky Way, but M83 also has a bar-like structure at its centre. In a barred spiral, the arms reach out from the ends of such a bar of stars.

The three frames were taken through blue, red and near-infrared filters and shown as blue, green and red. All three are available from the ESO Science Data Archive. The field covers about 6.8 by 6.8 arcminutes, recorded in frames of 2048 by 2048 pixels, with the atmosphere blurring the view by about 0.8 arcseconds on average.

understand.summary: FORS1 recorded blue light (B, shown blue), red light (R, shown green) and near-infrared light (I, shown red).
understand.eye: The I-band light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye.

alt: The central region of a barred spiral galaxy.

caption: The Tarantula Nebula region of the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, Chile
story: This wide colour view shows the Tarantula Nebula and its surroundings in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of our Milky Way about 170,000 light-years away in the southern constellation Dorado, the Swordfish. A few small areas near the edges lacked coverage in one or more of the three colours, so they appear black.

It combines 15 exposures in visible light, taken with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla Observatory. Five exposures each went through blue, visual and red filters, rendered as blue, green and red.

The field is large, about 34 by 34 arcminutes, and six smaller areas from it, each featuring particular objects, were released separately. The Tarantula Nebula itself is classified as an HII region, a cloud of gas lit up by hot young stars, whose radiation strips electrons from its hydrogen atoms and makes the gas glow.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager recorded B, V and R visible-light exposures, shown as blue, green and red.
understand.eye: Stacking many exposures of 200 seconds each collected far more light than the eye can gather.

alt: A wide field of the Large Magellanic Cloud around the Tarantula Nebula, with small black areas near the borders.

caption: The Cartwheel Galaxy and its companions, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Two rings dominate this Webb view of the Cartwheel Galaxy, a bright inner ring and a colourful outer one, joined by bright red streaks like the spokes of a wheel, with a companion spiral galaxy at the top left. The image combines Webb's Near-Infrared Camera and Mid-Infrared Instrument, revealing details that are hard to make out in either one alone.

The Cartwheel formed in a high-speed collision about 400 million years ago. Both rings are spreading outward from the site of the impact, like shockwaves. Much of the large spiral that existed before the crash still survives, however, including its rotating arms, which create the spokes. The red colour, in the Cartwheel and in the companion, comes from glowing dust rich in hydrocarbons.

Among the red swirls sit many blue dots, each a single star or a pocket where stars are forming. NIRCam also separates the older stars and dense dust in the core from the younger stars outside it. Webb has caught the galaxy in a very short-lived stage, and its final form remains a mystery.
explore: MIRI data are shown in orange and NIRCam data in blue, yellow and red. A University of Arizona team built NIRCam together with Lockheed Martin's Advanced Technology Center, while MIRI was contributed by ESA and NASA and built by a European consortium working with JPL and the University of Arizona.

understand.summary: Webb's MIRI data are coloured orange, while NIRCam data are coloured blue, yellow and red.
understand.eye: This near- and mid-infrared light is invisible to the human eye.

alt: A ring galaxy with a bright inner ring and a colourful outer ring linked by red spoke-like streaks and dotted with blue points, with a companion spiral galaxy at top left.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 300, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, Chile
story: This picture shows the southern spiral galaxy NGC 300, about 6 million light-years away in Sculptor, taken with the Wide Field Imager at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. It was pieced together from a great many separate frames taken through a wide range of filters, gathered over many observing nights across several years.

Most of the images went through red, green or blue filters. Special filters that pass only light from ionised hydrogen or oxygen were added to pick out the glowing clouds in the galaxy's spiral arms. Altogether, the exposures add up to around 50 hours.

The main aim of this long campaign was an unusually thorough census of the galaxy's stars, counting how many there are and of what kinds, and flagging regions, or even single stars, that deserve a closer and more focused look. A collection of data this rich should also prove useful in many other ways for years to come.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager recorded red, green and blue light plus hydrogen-alpha and oxygen filters. The exact colour mapping isn't published, though the gas filters highlight glowing clouds in the arms.
understand.eye: Around 50 hours of exposure gather far more light than an eye could.

alt: The spiral galaxy NGC 300 with glowing clouds along its spiral arms.

caption: The dwarf galaxy I Zwicky 18, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Concentrated bluish-white knots sit at the heart of this small galaxy, wrapped in wispy blue filaments, with a companion galaxy just above and to the left. This is I Zwicky 18, a dwarf irregular galaxy much smaller than our Milky Way, seen by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

Its youthful look resembles galaxies usually found only in the early universe, and it had been thought of as a toddler. But Hubble found faint, older stars inside, suggesting it may be as old as most other galaxies. White-reddish stars, perhaps as old as 10 billion years, appear in both I Zwicky 18 and its companion. The companion's gravitational tug may have triggered the recent star formation behind the galaxy's young appearance.

The two knots are major starburst regions. The blue filaments are gas bubbles blown out by winds and supernovae from an earlier generation of hot young stars, now heated by ultraviolet light from newer ones.
explore: Hubble also identified Cepheid variable stars in the galaxy for the first time, which put its distance at 59 million light-years, nearly 10 million light-years beyond earlier estimates. The reddish extended objects around the pair are ancient, fully formed galaxies far in the background.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys image combines observations through two filters, described as blue and red. The exact colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal faint, old stars the eye could never pick out.

alt: A small galaxy with two bluish-white knots at its centre, wispy blue filaments around them, a companion galaxy to the upper left and reddish distant galaxies around.

caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 66 (NGC 3627), imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Large-scale dust lanes wind through this spiral galaxy, which has a well-developed central bulge and many regions of warm hydrogen gas scattered across its disc. This is NGC 3627, also known as Messier 66, in the constellation Leo, the Lion, imaged with ESO's Very Large Telescope.

Radiation from clusters of newborn stars is ionising these hydrogen regions, and very active star formation is probably also going on in the galaxy's nuclear regions. M66 is the largest member of the Leo Triplet, alongside M 65 and NGC 3628, all three about 35 million light-years away.

Its spiral arms look distorted and lifted above the galaxy's main plane. The lopsided look is probably the result of gravitational tugging by the other two galaxies. The galaxy's number comes from its place as the 66th object in Charles Messier's famous catalogue of nebulae.
explore: The photo was made with the FORS1 and FORS2 instruments on the VLT's MELIPAL and YEPUN telescopes, combining three exposures in different wavebands. Charles Messier, the French astronomer who compiled the catalogue, lived from 1730 to 1817.

understand.summary: FORS1 and FORS2 on the Very Large Telescope recorded blue (B), visual (V) and red (R) exposures. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal faint dust lanes and gas regions beyond what the eye would see.

alt: A spiral galaxy with a well-developed central bulge, prominent dust lanes and glowing gas regions across its disc.

caption: Barnard's Galaxy (NGC 6822), imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, Chile
story: Reddish nebulae are scattered across this dwarf galaxy, and a prominent bubble-shaped nebula stands out at upper left. This is Barnard's Galaxy, also known as NGC 6822, a dwarf irregular galaxy that is one of the Milky Way's neighbours, about 2 million light-years away in Sagittarius. It was photographed with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla in northern Chile.

The red nebulae are regions of active star formation, where young, hot stars heat the gas clouds around them. At the heart of the bubble, a group of massive, blazing stars drives waves of matter into the surrounding interstellar material, creating a glowing structure that looks ring-shaped from our viewpoint.

Other ripples of heated matter, thrown out by energetic young stars, are dotted across the galaxy. The image combines data through four filters, B, V, R and H-alpha, over a field of 35 by 34 arcminutes.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager recorded B, V, R and hydrogen-alpha light. The colour mapping isn't published, though star-forming nebulae appear reddish.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates glowing gas, and long exposures reveal much more than the eye could.

alt: A dwarf galaxy with scattered reddish nebulae and a bubble-shaped ring nebula at upper left.

caption: The galaxies NGC 4302 and NGC 4298, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two galaxies share this Hubble view. NGC 4298, seen almost face-on, displays its spiral arms, dotted with blue areas of young stars where star birth is still going on. Its neighbour NGC 4302, seen edge-on, has a disc mottled brown by vast swathes of dust, with a burst of blue on its left side marking a region of very vigorous star formation. Both lie 55 million light-years away.
The pair were observed to celebrate Hubble's 27th year in orbit. The result is a mosaic of four separate Hubble captures stitched together to cover this wide field.

Visible and near-infrared light from the galaxies was combined to produce the colours, all captured by Wide Field Camera 3. The face-on view of NGC 4298 lays out its spiral arms, while in the edge-on NGC 4302 the dust in the disc dominates.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 combined visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared component is invisible to the eye.

alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with blue star-forming patches beside an edge-on galaxy with brown dust and a blue burst on its left side.

caption: The galaxy pair Arp 116, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the peculiar galaxy pair Arp 116, made up of a giant elliptical galaxy, Messier 60, and a much smaller spiral, NGC 4647. They lie about 50 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo.

Astronomers have long debated whether the two are really interacting. They overlap as seen from Earth, but there is no sign of fresh star birth, and that would be among the clearest clues of an interaction. Recent studies of very detailed Hubble images, however, suggest that some tidal interaction may be beginning.

Just below and to the right of M60 sits an even smaller neighbour, M60-UCD1, only 1/500th the diameter of the Milky Way. It is densely packed, with about 140 million stars squeezed into just 300 light-years, and astronomers have found a supermassive black hole with the mass of 20 million Suns at its centre.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS and WFPC2 observed in blue, visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and near-infrared light reveal detail beyond the reach of the eye.

alt: A large elliptical galaxy overlapping a smaller spiral galaxy, with a tiny compact galaxy below and to the right.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 253, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This sky field centres on NGC 253, a type Sc spiral galaxy seen nearly edge-on in the southern constellation Sculptor, about 8 million light-years away. Many of the numerous small, slightly fuzzy objects around it are almost certainly globular clusters belonging to NGC 253.

The image adds together five exposures, each 5 minutes long, all taken through a blue filter. They were shifted slightly relative to one another so that the small gaps between the eight CCD detectors in the camera's mosaic no longer show.

Faint trails left by 2 artificial satellites also cross the frame. Before the exposures were combined, they were processed to remove the detector's baseline signal and correct its uneven sensitivity, and some faulty columns of pixels were filled in by interpolation. A globular cluster, for reference, is a dense ball of old stars, and large galaxies are often surrounded by many of them, which is why so many faint dots crowd the space around this one.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope recorded this through a single blue (B-band) filter, so the image has no separate colour channels.
understand.eye: Summing five exposures collects far more light than the eye can, revealing faint globular clusters.

alt: A nearly edge-on spiral galaxy in a star field, with small fuzzy globular clusters around it and faint satellite trails.

caption: The elliptical galaxy ESO 306-17, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This image from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys highlights the large, bright elliptical galaxy ESO 306-17 in the southern sky, about 500 million light-years away in the constellation Columba. It seems to be surrounded by other galaxies, but the bright ones at bottom left are thought to lie in the foreground rather than at the same distance.

In fact, ESO 306-17 sits largely on its own, surrounded by a vast expanse of hot gas and dark matter. It belongs to what astronomers call a fossil group, a very different setting from a crowded cluster of galaxies.

Researchers are also using the Hubble data to hunt for nearby ultra-compact dwarf galaxies. These are miniature dwarfs stripped down to little more than their cores by encounters with larger, more powerful galaxies. Most found so far sit near giant ellipticals in large galaxy clusters, so researchers want to know whether similar objects also turn up in a fossil group like this one.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue and near-infrared filters, with a synthetic green channel. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and near-infrared light reveal faint galaxies the eye couldn't see.

alt: A large, bright elliptical galaxy with several brighter foreground galaxies at bottom left.

caption: Pandora's Cluster (Abell 2744), imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A foreground star with Webb's distinctive diffraction spikes dominates this crowded field just right of centre, while larger white hazy blobs gather in three areas and countless smaller sources, many red or orange, fill the gaps. The hazy white blobs are the galaxies of Pandora's Cluster, Abell 2744, about 3 billion light-years away, seen by Webb's NIRCam.

Pandora's Cluster is several already-massive galaxy clusters coming together into a mega cluster. Its mass is so concentrated that gravity warps spacetime, creating a natural magnifying glass, a gravitational lens, that lets astronomers see very distant light sources beyond it that would otherwise be undetectable, even to Webb.

Those lensed sources appear red, often stretched into arcs. Many are galaxies from the early universe, magnified for astronomers to study. In all, astronomers estimate that 50 000 sources of near-infrared light appear in this single image, their light having crossed a wide range of distances to reach Webb.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed in near-infrared light. Blue shows the shortest wavelengths, green intermediate ones and red the longest.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and many lensed galaxies here would be undetectable without the cluster's magnification.

alt: A crowded galaxy field with a large spiked star just right of centre, three areas of large white hazy galaxies, and many smaller white, red and orange sources.

caption: The giant elliptical galaxy M87, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Amid a smooth yellow glow of older stars, a soft blue jet and a swarm of star-like globular clusters stand out in this Hubble image. The galaxy is M87, a huge elliptical in Virgo, a constellation of the spring sky, some 54 million light-years from the Sun, home to several trillion stars, a supermassive black hole and some 13,000 globular clusters.

The jet is a stream of material driven by the black hole and flung out from the galaxy's core. As gas from the centre falls onto the black hole, the energy set free powers a fire-hose jet of subatomic particles, accelerated to nearly the speed of light.

M87 dominates the heart of the Virgo Cluster, which holds some 2,000 galaxies, and it measures 120,000 light-years across. From that central position it may have gathered some of its globular clusters by pulling them away from nearby dwarf galaxies, which now seem to have none of their own.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed in blue, visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published, though older stars appear yellow and the jet blue.
understand.eye: Long exposures and near-infrared light reveal faint clusters beyond the reach of the eye.

alt: A large, smooth yellow elliptical galaxy with a soft blue jet from its core and many star-like globular clusters around it.

caption: The giant elliptical galaxy NGC 1132, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thousands of ancient globular clusters swarm around the giant elliptical galaxy NGC 1132 like bees around a hive in this Hubble image, with many far more distant galaxies scattered in the background. NGC 1132 lies about 300 million light-years away in the constellation Eridanus.

It is probably a fossil, the remains of a huge pile-up in which galaxy after galaxy collided and merged, building a brilliant but fuzzy giant elliptical that far outshines typical galaxies. Together with the small dwarf galaxies around it, NGC 1132 is described as a fossil group, because the whole system is probably the remnant of a group of galaxies that merged in the recent past.
The globular clusters are likely survivors from the galaxies NGC 1132 has swallowed. Because they outlasted their parent galaxies, they may preserve a record of how this giant was assembled.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue and near-infrared filters, with a synthetic green channel. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal faint globular clusters and distant galaxies that the eye couldn't see.

alt: A giant fuzzy elliptical galaxy surrounded by thousands of tiny globular clusters, with many distant galaxies in the background.

caption: The starburst galaxy NGC 4666, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, Chile
story: This visible-light image shows the galaxy NGC 4666 at its centre, with its neighbour NGC 4668 visible to the lower left. Lying around 80 million light-years from Earth, NGC 4666 is a starburst galaxy, where especially intense star formation is under way. The picture comes from the Wide Field Imager, a camera on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile.

The starburst is thought to have been set off by gravitational interactions with neighbouring galaxies, NGC 4668 among them. Supernova explosions and powerful winds from massive stars in the starburst region together push an immense stream of gas out of the galaxy and into space, an outflow known as a superwind.

ESA's XMM-Newton space telescope had earlier observed NGC 4666 in X-rays. These visible-light observations were made to follow up background objects spotted in those X-ray images. The field covers 16 by 12 arcminutes and combines twelve CCD frames of 67 megapixels each, shot through filters for blue, green and red light.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager recorded visible light through blue, green and red filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures gather more light than the eye can.

alt: A galaxy at the centre of the frame, with a neighbouring galaxy to the lower left.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1097, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This nearly true-colour view shows the spiral galaxy NGC 1097, about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Fornax. It was made with the VIMOS instrument on Melipal, the 8.2-metre Unit Telescope 3, part of ESO's Very Large Telescope.

Three wavebands were used, with R-band shown as red, V as green and B as blue. Because the colours follow the order of the wavelengths, the result is close to what our eyes would perceive, only far deeper. Observing conditions were very good, with seeing, the blurring caused by the atmosphere, well below 1 arcsecond.

The images were taken on the night of 9 to 10 December 2004, with Chile's President Ricardo Lagos present at the observatory. Exposure times were short, at 2.25 minutes in R, 3 in V and 6 in B. Astronomers from ESO's Paranal science operations took and pre-processed all the exposures, and the image covers 7.7 by 6.6 arcminutes of sky.

understand.summary: VIMOS recorded R-band light (shown red), V-band light (green) and B-band light (blue), giving an almost-true colour composite.
understand.eye: The colours are close to natural, but the telescope gathers far more light than the eye, revealing faint detail.

alt: The spiral galaxy NGC 1097 in near-true colour.

caption: The galaxy group Hickson Compact Group 90, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Three galaxies share this Hubble view, with NGC 7173 at middle left, NGC 7174 at middle right and NGC 7176 at lower right. They belong to Hickson Compact Group 90, about 120 million light-years away in Piscis Austrinus, named after the astronomer Paul Hickson, who first catalogued compact groups like this one during the 1980s.

NGC 7173 and NGC 7176 look like smooth, ordinary elliptical galaxies without much gas or dust. An elliptical galaxy is a rounded collection of stars with little of the raw material that fuels new star formation. NGC 7174 is very different, a mangled spiral barely holding on as a separate galaxy while its close neighbours tear it apart.

The strong tidal forces running through the group have pulled large numbers of stars away from their home galaxies. Those stars are now spread thinly, forming a faint, glowing component that belongs to the group as a whole rather than to any one galaxy.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue and near-infrared filters, with a synthetic green channel. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal the faint glow of scattered stars that the eye would miss.

alt: Three galaxies, two smooth ellipticals at middle left and lower right and a distorted spiral at middle right being pulled apart.

caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 83, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, Chile
story: This image of the galaxy Messier 83 was taken with the Wide Field Imager at La Silla, an ESO observatory high in the dry mountains of Chile's Atacama Desert. The galaxy lies roughly 15 million light-years away, toward the huge southern constellation Hydra, the Sea Serpent.

Messier 83 stretches over 40 000 light-years, which makes it about 2.5 times smaller than our Milky Way. In some ways, though, the two are quite alike. Both have a bar across the nucleus, the dense, rounded concentration of stars at a galaxy's centre.

A bar is a straight structure of stars running through a spiral galaxy's middle, and the spiral arms extend from its ends. We live inside the Milky Way, so we can never view its bar from outside, but galaxies such as Messier 83 show what a similar structure looks like from afar.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager recorded blue, visual and red light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal more of the galaxy's faint outer regions than the eye could.

alt: The barred spiral galaxy Messier 83.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 3190, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Tightly wound arms and a warped shape make this edge-on spiral look like a gigantic potato crisp. This is NGC 3190, about 60 million light-years away in Leo, seen with ESO's Very Large Telescope. In the galaxy's south-western part, its dust lanes form a V shape.

Two supernovae appeared in this galaxy. SN 2002bo sits between the arms of that V. The second, SN 2002cv, is hidden behind so much dust that it cannot be seen, although its position is marked on the image.

The observations were part of a programme to study the physics of Type Ia supernovae. The colour composite brings together 14 minutes of exposures through B, V, R and I filters, taken with FORS1 on the VLT's Kueyen unit, and the field of view is 6.15 by 5 arcminutes. The data were extracted from the archive, reduced and colour-processed by Henri Boffin of ESO.

understand.summary: FORS1 on the VLT's Kueyen unit observed through B, V, R and I filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and near-infrared I-band light reveal detail the eye can't, though one supernova stays hidden behind dust.

alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy with a warped shape and dark dust lanes forming a V, with a supernova position marked.

caption: The Small Magellanic Cloud, imaged by ESO's VISTA telescope
story: Millions of stars fill every part of this frame, a very wide infrared view of the Small Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy about 200,000 light-years away in Tucana. It was taken with ESO's VISTA survey telescope and is the biggest infrared image ever made of the SMC.

The SMC stands out in the southern sky and is visible without any telescope. However, clouds of interstellar dust keep visible-light telescopes from getting a really clear look at what lies inside it. VISTA's infrared capabilities let astronomers see the galaxy's countless stars far more clearly than ever before.

Besides the SMC itself, VISTA picked up plenty of background galaxies and a number of star clusters, among them the very bright globular cluster 47 Tucanae on the right. A globular cluster is a dense ball of old stars.

understand.summary: VISTA's VIRCAM camera observed in near-infrared light through Y, J and Ks filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The SMC is visible to the unaided eye, but this near-infrared view sees through dust that hides many of its stars in visible light.

alt: A wide field crowded with millions of stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, with a bright globular cluster at the right.
